#4044. Demanding 300GB to install despite its actual size of 145GB, Phantom Blade Zero makes me question what a gigabyte is worth

We're not in a very cheap era for PC parts. A (possibly manufactured!) GPU shortage making cards that can actually run modern games near-inaccessible to the vast majority of people, combined with RAM and SSDs just generally being horrifically expensive due to demand for their use in data centers, is making contemporary games with high performance requirements very difficult for some people to justify even trying to run, let alone buy. S-Game's recent reveal of wuxia action game Phantom Blade Zero's preload guide and system requirements has brought this to mind, alongside bringing tears to my eyes, as the game requires not only an SSD to run at all, and 145GB to install, but 300GB of free space to pre-load.

Genuinely, what are we doing here. The guide states that this is because "temporary files and the complete game must coexist during the unlock process", and that "once the process is complete, storage usage will drop to approximately 145GB." Oh, sure, just a small install then. 145GB is already a ridiculous size for one game — I know that commenters will tell me that this has become somewhat standard, but that is not reasonable or a good thing — and requiring players to free up double the actual install size just to get the damn thing on your system remains absurd. Deputy ed/former hardware ed James says this is probably a quirk of how Unreal Engine 5, specifically, handles updates. I asked him if there was anything else wrong with UE5 and he began staring into space.

Anyway, there's a lot of things that happen in games that makes me say something along the lines of 'fuck'. Constant layoffs, AI's tendrils being spread everywhere, CEOs telling me and their staff that it'll save their company. But this is something different, in which I stare at my monitor, read those system requirements again and just want to scream 'what the FUCK?' Phantom Blade Zero could be the greatest game ever made (it seems to be pretty good, if the recent reviews are anything to go by), but no game could ever be worth 300GB. Again, what are we doing. That's like, uh, sixty Devil May Cry 3s.

#4043. Phantom Blade Zero isn't even out yet, but it could be 'one of the year's breakout hits' as it shifts half a million copies on Steam alone

Chinese action game Phantom Blade Zero already appears to be outperforming massive games like Gears of War: E-Day and Control Resonant on Steam, despite still being days from release.

That's according to sales data scrutinised by Alinea Analytics head of market analysis Rhys Elliott, who posted their findings on LinkedIn. Based on Elliott's estimates, Phantom Blade Zero has already sold 500,000 copies on Steam through pre-orders, bringing in roughly $24m in revenue ahead of its launch next week. Elliott noted the figures meant Phantom Blade Zero was "outperforming" Gears of War: E-Day and Control Resonant on Steam at the time of writing, and that China is currently its top market.

Other interesting tidbits include the fact that Phantom Blade Zero has also generated a lofty 2.5m Steam wishlists. According to Elliott, 41 percent of players who've wishlisted the game have also played Black Myth Wukong, while 38 percent of them have played Elden Ring and 28 percent played Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice.

It's an impressive start for Phantom Blade Zero on PC, and Elliott goes on to say that "pre-launch signals" point to the game being popular on PS5 too. He even goes as far as to suggest it has the "potential to be one of the year's breakout single-player hits."

These figures emerge at a time China's games industry is enjoying a boom, and an increasing number of releases from Chinese developers are launching to critical and commercial success worldwide. Phantom Blade Zero has all the signs of becoming another hit it launches for PS5 and PC on 28th October.

#4042. Former Xbox Manager Explains Why $500M Cost For Gears: E-Day Doesn't Tell The Whole Story

Update [Mon 2nd Nov 2026, 1pm]: Windows Central's Jez Corden has weighed in with a few extra details this morning as well, explaining that according to a "variety of trusted sources", The Coalition has been contributing to many other Xbox projects over the past 6-7 years.

All of these seemingly factor into the $500M budget that has been attributed, although it's unknown to what extent.

"...The Coalition worked for over a year and a half on a prototype project for Xbox that Windows Central understands was ultimately canceled. The Coalition also worked on Avowed, Hellblade 2, Clockwork Revolution, State of Decay 3, Grounded and Grounded 2, and has even contributed to the upcoming StarCraft reboot."

"The Coalition also spent a great deal of time working with Epic Games on the "Matrix Awakens" Unreal Engine demonstration, as well as the Alpha Point demo, both of which were intended to showcase the potential of UE5 on next-gen consoles and PCs."

Nevertheless, Corden warns that $500 million is a "lot of money to invest without a specific structure in place to explain why some of these costs were worthwhile to Microsoft auditors", and that there have even been "some internal disagreements over how exactly attribution should be distributed".

Original Story: Over the past couple of weeks, there's been a lot of chatter about a rumoured $500 million cost for The Coalition to make Gears of War: E-Day, alongside debates about how much of that money went on the game itself.

Speaking on the weekend, former Xbox exec Derek Reese shared his take on the situation, suggesting that The Coalition is heavily involved with supporting Microsoft's branch of the Unreal Engine, which is where a lot of the cost goes.

Here's what the ex-Senior Product Manager of Xbox Game Services had to say:

So much of that cost is The Coalition being on the hook for the Microsoft branch of Unreal and one of the flagship titles. I should know, I tried to get leadership to support a plan to have other studios adopt it and write off the support costs. Same problem with Turn10 and ForzaTech.

This aligns with what Jez Corden of Windows Central was saying a few weeks ago as well, who originally suggested that because The Coalition is "the technological glue for all of Xbox", some of that money is "spread across the entire portfolio" and even goes towards The Coalition's help on other Xbox games like Fable and Forza Horizon.

Corden confirmed yesterday that Reese's comments align with what he's heard:

In some follow-up posts, Reese mentioned that he thinks The Coalition "accomplished their end goals very well and delivered a great accomplishment in E-Day", while also suggesting that there's a "publicly visible pattern of allowing departments to shoulder the costs of leadership direction", pointing to Double Fine as a recent notable example.

So, hopefully we can put this one to bed now! It seems the $500 million budget IS a legit figure for Gears of War: E-Day, but it's hard to realistically attribute that entire figure to the game itself.

The big question is what Xbox thinks about all of this, including whether the game has been a success in terms of sales, Premium Upgrade conversions, Xbox Game Pass subscriptions and its pulling power as an Xbox console exclusive, and it could be some time until we know the answer to that.

ANY well managed corporation has a time management system where employees and contractors register their time and what project they were working on. #4041. Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced is wrapping things up with one last big update that adds in new game plus and a throwback to the original game

Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced is setting sail for quieter pastures. That's because the game's last big update arrived today, with Ubisoft explaining that there are only plans for quality-of-life updates for the game going forward. Still, it's a meaty enough sounding update, and one that could in theory keep you going forever if you'd like to torture yourself by relegating your life to a single video game.

Well, maybe not forever. This update is introducing new game plus, letting you replay the game from the start, if you're the kind of person that somehow has time for that. It'll be possible to do this up to five times, with each subsequent playthrough increasing the difficulty level. You'll get to hang on to things like tools, weapons, upgrades for the Jackdaw, outfits, hideout progression, codex items and more besides.

With new game plus also comes a new difficulty setting, nightmare mode, which "transforms Black Flag Resynced into a brutal fight for survival where every duel can be your last. Enemies react faster, hit harder, and punish hesitation. The Caribbean is as beautiful as ever, but beneath the waves and beyond the horizon, death awaits the unprepared." Parrying timing is also reduced in this mode, there's no more white glint on enemy attacks, and the one-shot kill safety is disabled. On the stealth front, deduction time is greatly reduced and enemies can hear you when you're moving faster than anything above a walk.

Beyond this, a number of community chests have been hidden around the game, "some with special community requested rewards." You can also expect some new, or technically old, takedowns; "We have brought back takedown animations from the original game, including hidden blade, unarmed, single sword and gunblade takedowns." There's also some new cosmetics, and a good range of bug fixes. You can read about all of that over on Ubisoft's website.

This all comes the same month that Ubisoft laid off 70 workers at Ubisoft Singapore, the lead developer on Black Flag Resynced. Solidarity with all those affected.

#4040. Half-Life 3 is back in the news again as Valve developer accidentally sort-of references it in public, reigniting hope once more

It's been 19 years since the release of Half-Life 2: Episode 2, and yet the ceaseless clamour for a Valve game with a number '3' in its title continues. And following a swell of reports suggesting Half-Life 3 isn't just real, its development is well underway, a Valve developer has gone and sent the internet a-chatter all over again by publicly, albeit accidentally, referencing its codename during a livestream.

Valve's first attempt at releasing a Half-Life game with a '3' in its name would have been the ill-fated Half-Life 2: Episode 3, which was abandoned - despite Valve previously announcing it as part of a planned trilogy - sometime around 2009. After that, the studio seemingly had a crack at making a full-blown sequel, with Valve boss Gabe Newell confirming a few years back that Half-Life 3 had been in development around 2013/2014, but was ultimately scrapped because it was built on the unfinished Source 2 engine.

Sometime in 2021, however, dataminers began to notice something interesting: repeated references to a project codenamed "HLX" in Valve-related files. Inevitably, this led to a frenzy of speculation that Valve might finally be reviving its long-anticipated first-person shooter sequel. And evidence has seemingly continued to amass over time. In 2024, for instance, Valve insider Tyler McVicker shared some of his datamined findings, claiming what he'd found pointed to a new "fully-fledged Half-Life game" - a claim coinciding with a leak from an actor likely involved in the project.

It all reached something of a crescendo when McVicker released a new video last year suggesting the rumoured Half-Life 3 was now "playable, end-to-end", and claimed it could even release before 2025 was through. Fans, meanwhile, did some sleuthing and concluded Half-Life 3 would likely launch in either November or December last year. All of this, clearly, did not come to pass, and the Half-Life 3 hype has died down a little since then. And yet here we are again, with the latest twist in the saga being a public reference to the codenamed 'HLX' by a Valve developer, albeit seemingly accidentally.

Let us jump to a recent GameSoundCon Q&A panel (promptly clipped and shared by McVicker again), in which Valve's music designer Mike Morasky spent some time discussing the audio work on the company's games. "Deadlock has their own version of HDR," Morasky explained, "HLX has its own version, and so on and so forth." Midway through the sentence, Morasky seems to taper off, as if immediately realising the error of his ways. Soon after, Valve sound designer David Feise appears to lean over and whisper "nice work", which some have understandably taken to be sarcasm.

So what does all this tell us? Not a lot, really, beyond the fact it suggests HLX is a thing (which we mostly already knew) and that it's still being worked on. Morasky's framing would, however, also suggest that whatever HLX is, it's a standalone project, and one requiring music at that. So I guess those Half-Life 3 dreams can live on for another day. The only question remaining, which will arrive first: Half-Life 3 or the heat death of the sun?

#4039. Final Fantasy Resonance Producer Had to Fight Square Enix Execs Who Wanted Cheap Port of Dead Mobile Game

Final Fantasy Resonance has seemingly gone down really, really well with fans of the franchise — and so it's surprising to hear that Square Enix's leadership were apparently against the idea of the game.

Resonance is very much a callback to classic Final Fantasy in terms of gameplay and structure; some would go as far to argue that it's just what the property needs at this point.

The recently released and highly rated RPG is built on the bones of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius — the mobile gacha game that was shut down back in 2024.

However, Resonance reworks entire systems to ensure that everything functions as you'd expect of a traditional Final Fantasy adventure. After playing it myself for review, it's clear that the development team put a lot of effort into essentially remaking Exvius.

But according to project producer Keisuke Nakashima, his higher-ups wanted a simple port of Exvius rather than the extensive adaptation that we ended up with.

Review Final Fantasy Resonance (PS5) - Square's Series Returns to Its Roots to Fantastic Effect

He told Bloomberg (via Nintendo Everything): "Initially there was some resistance to the idea from Square Enix executives [...] I didn’t want to go down that route. I wanted to create an original version for consoles that was a full-blown gameplay experience.”

The suggestion is that a straightforward port would have cost much less to produce. At the time of writing, we don't know how well Resonance has sold.

Still, I'm glad Nakashima held his ground, because I'm not even sure how an Exvius port would have worked in the first place. It certainly wouldn't have hit like Resonance does.

Have you been playing Final Fantasy Resonance? What do you think of it? Protect those crystals at all costs in the comments section below.

A new Batman 2 leak has hit the internet, and it might confirm some fascinating details about the upcoming DC movie.

Now, persistent rumors have been circulating that Sebastian Stan is not playing Two-Face, as reported, but is instead playing Victor Zsasz – the terrifying, bald serial killer who keeps a tally of his victims on his body.

The facial mold that looks like Brian Tyree Henry, meanwhile, bears a strong resemblance to Two-Face. While the disfigurement doesn't look too extreme, his upper lip is seriously wounded in a pattern that mirrors the character's look in Batman: The Animated Series. This would suggest that it's Henry, not Stan, playing the iconic villain.

The Court of Owls – a sinister group of Gotham's elite who wear creepy owl masks and control the city from the shadows – has also been heavily speculated to be part of the film, and the "Owl" container seems to confirm they'll factor in somehow. #4037. A leaked trailer for Transformers: Reactivate shows off the only lick of gameplay we'll likely ever see of the cancelled co-op action game

Back in 2022, Gears Tactics studio Splash Damage revealed that they were working on a Transformers game. It was called Transformers: Reactivate, and at the time was set to be a 1-4 player co-op action game, but come 2025 and the game gets canned all while parent company Tencent was going on a funding withdrawal spree in the games industry. Nothing substantial was ever really shown off of the game, but a trailer has now been leaked featuring what was apparently meant to be an internal look at it in action.

The trailer was shared by a Gwitter user called Nem who is devoted to "archiving and preserving Transformers: Reactivate because I need to cope somehow." Prior to the trailer itself, a message from Nem explained: "The following is an internal trailer not meant for the public, the music in it was released on October 21st 2024, placing this trailer at most three months prior to cancellation. With Tencent having pulled out in June/July 2024, this leads us to believe this trailer was made as part of an investment pitch to other publishers that ultimately failed."

Full credit for this discovery goes to @EnderGuyZV2!! TRANSFORMERS REACTIVATE GAMEPLAY TRAILER!!From around October-November 2024! This is our first glimpse at what the $70 game was hoping for, and hopefully we learn more about this version as time goes on. pic.twitter.com/52GhgTUrtz

Apparently by the time this trailer had been made, the game had shifted gears into a premium release, moving away from being a free-to-play live service game, complete with a story campaign that could be played solo or in online co-op. And the result is certainly a fairly real looking 2020s video game, at the very least. It's got some shooting, it's got some driving, it's got some shooting while driving, though it has surprisingly little actual transforming. Perhaps they were still ironing out the kinks mechanically and animationally.

This is one of those weird things where a big licensed game feels like it should have been a slam dunk, if only it had come out 10 years prior and wasn't catered towards the curse that is live service in the first place. I'm also always oddly eeked out by leaked trailers, not from some weird moral perspective, but because it's evidence of something existing, and yet is entirely impossible to engage with. What other medium has anything like this? Weird! I look forward to someone figuring out the solution to this. I'd suggest starting with dismantling capitalism, perhaps.

#4036. "Why the f**k would they add a perk like that?" - Modern Warfare 4 DMZ players are up in arms over the ability to self-revive

Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction shooter mode has only been out for two days - and only for those who pre-ordered the game - but already players are up in arms over a particular trait that allows competitors to revive themselves after being killed.

That trait is called Possum, and is one of the many abilities players can unlock as they level up their operators. How it works is this: if the trait is active, you're given the option, once per match, to revive yourself on command when killed. Doing so places you in a Last Stand state, and you'll need to pick yourself up from this vulnerable downed position to continue playing. All together, getting back into the firefight from dead takes around 10 uninterrupted seconds. You also lose any loot you've gathered when you revive - so you're back to square one.

It goes without saying that the ability to come back to life at all in an extraction shooter is a bold addition to DMZ. There doesn't seem to be a great way to see if a dead opponent has it, meaning every player you kill could come back for revenge later in the match when your guard is down. It doesn't take long to unlock either! If you focus your operator progression solely on the Warfighter path, Possum can be unlocked in a handful of hours. As such, it's likely someone in a DMZ match will be ready to pounce. And to say Possum is proving divisive among Call of Duty players would be an understatement.

"Possum is garbage and needs to be deleted ASAP," pdmaloney94 wrote on the DMZ subreddit. This mechanic breaks DMZ in my opinion and severely takes the stakes out of [matches]. After fully killing a team we now have to babysit their corpses until we can confirm that they returned to the lobby? Who on earth thought this was a good idea to implement into an extraction shooter?"

That sentiment was mirrored by other players too. "I just clutched a 1v3 in the underground mall, go to revive my teammate before looting anyone, and the first person I killed is laying in the corner and kills me, "SkinDiesel wrote. "Why the f**k would they add a perk like that to an extraction shooter? I get the self-revives and tourniquets, but reviving yourself from death for free every single game is diabolical."

Some players pushed back, however, offering a more measured evaluation of Possum and some strategies to counter it. "Just move on and they won’t catch you because they have no loot to pursue," suggested cleppingout. Wilus82 brought up an interesting idea too: "I was reading that people were saying to put trip mines or land mines on their bodies."

Already, prominent Call of Duty YouTubers are decrying the trait. Phixate lambasted it as "completely broken", while Wynn-Gaming called Possum "crazy" - the trait drawing criticism largely due to its potential impact on team-vs-team gunfights. After all, pushing toward a team once you take down one of their members and thin out the ranks is a strategy as old as time. If that apparent numbers advantage suddenly evaporates mid-conflict, it's potentially a big deal.

My take? I hope Possum doesn't get nerfed, at least for a few weeks. Let it ride. Already we're seeing the way it's encouraging players to adopt interesting new strategies, and two days isn't nearly enough time to determine whether the trait is genuinely broken. Let the meta game settle, allow people to push it to its limits, then, if it remains a problem by December, call pest patrol on the possum.

DMZ's new trait isn't the only thing raising eyebrows, of course.. Players have been spawning in the middle of roads and immediately getting run over, which is hilarious. It'll be interesting to see what else emerges when the wider populace gains access later today.

#4035. Mass Effect crossover items have seemingly been removed from Battlefield 6 following EA's sudden closure of BioWare

After EA's sudden shutdown of developer BioWare, upcoming crossover items themed around Mass Effect appear to have been removed from Battlefield 6.

When Battlefield 6's Season Five dropped earlier this month, many eager fans spotted that a collection of Mass Effect items had sneakily been added to the shooter's cosmetic menus, but were still unavailable to unlock or buy. The cosmetics included a little Normandy ship charm that dangled off weapons, some weapons that wouldn't look out of place in Mass Effect's sci-fi world and a few N7 tags. (Good spot, IGN!)

DICE has quietly removed all 'Mass Effect' cosmetics from #Battlefield6 after BioWare closure. Player card backgrounds, weapon skins, weapon charms, weapon stickers, sprays, soldier patches... everything. https://t.co/8KkjOm8nX2

With N7 Day right around the corner - slated for the 7th of November, as per usual - series fans reckoned the items would serve to celebrate the series' annual tradition and perhaps herald more news of Mass Effect 5. Those hopes were short-lived, sadly - developer BioWare is no more and the next Mass Effect game has been cancelled.

Following the shock closure, all Mass Effect items have seemingly been scrubbed from Battlefield 6's menus. Players spotted their absence in no time and shared the news online.

Battlefield 6's recent Dead Space crossover event already invited lots of divided opinions, with some players upset that the widely loved horror series is stuck in limbo while EA uses it to feed its live-service machine. Perhaps pulling a similar trick with Mass Effect - by celebrating N7 Day despite the series' uncertain future - would've simply poured salt onto a freshly opened wound. Although, the cosmetics were seemingly finished and ready to go.

In its announcement memo, EA said it was "making deliberate choices to align talent and investment where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth" - hence the decision to lay off 400 workers and cut BioWare entirely. The games industry has since mourned the loss of a beloved, long-standing role-playing institution.

A former BioWare dev recently claimed Mass Effect 5 would've borrowed from Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher to deliver unprecedented player choice. We'll never know for sure what BioWare would've cooked up, but a leaked trailer for Mass Effect Universe gives us a taste - a small, bittersweet, neon-drenched taste.

EA itself was recently taken private by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Jared Kushner's private equity group Affinity Partners and Silver Lake in a $55bn leveraged buyout.

#4034. UK-based Rockstar devs will be putting their union recognition to a vote during GTA 6's launch next month

The vote will also be held when closing arguments will be made for the ongoing employment tribunal

November is potentially going to be big for Rockstar Games, and not just because of that GTA 6 thing they're doing. As shared in a press release from the Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB), recognition of the IWGB Union at Rockstar will be voted upon by staffers at the studio, with votes being held from November 12th (a week before GTA 6's launch date) and November 26th.

"The terms of the recognition deal, agreed upon by workers and management, would give workers a say over topics including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies," the press release explains. It also notes that if the vote is successful, the union will become the largest recognised union in the UK games industry.

This also comes at another pivotal time for Rockstar workers, both current and former alike. Almost exactly a year ago, Rockstar laid off 31 staffers in an alleged act of union busting. Fast forward to now, and an employment tribunal is being held between the game developer, the IWGB, and the laid off workers. Closing arguments for the tribunal will take place between November 17th and 18th, mere days ahead of the game's launch. It'll still be a while until a judge decides if Rockstar did break employment law.

In a statement, Rockstar Game Workers Union Committee Member Shanti Easton-Steel said, "For me, this vote comes down to ensuring employees at Rockstar get honesty and openness surrounding the decisions that affect them. When management choices are kept hidden, we can’t properly address issues like the gender pay gap, the uneven and ever-changing policies on overtime pay, or the concerns many co-workers hold around job security post-release."

Solidarity with the workers as always. GTA 6 will undoubtedly be the biggest game of the decade, and everyone that has worked on it deserves to be properly compensated and assuaged of their concerns.

It should also prevent vibe-coded game recompilations and PC ports, like the viral AI-fuelled Bloodborne project

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As vibe-coded game recompilations and PC ports take over the scene, Claude AI developer Anthropic has added a new rule to its code to stop users from "recreating someone else's specific game" in an attempt to prevent IP infringement when using the technology that rips from others' work.

Revealed in a post on Twitter by Anthropic member of technical staff Addy Osmani, while "original games" based on users' own ideas can still be AI-generated, recreations of existing ones should no longer be permitted.

"We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Osmani explains. "Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working."

The new rule itself, highlighted on Twitter by user chasm, reads: "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets. Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."

Obviously, it remains to be seen whether this'll work as intended or if folks will find a way around the restriction. Osmani notes that Anthropic is trying to strike "the right balance," and for now, "if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way."

In theory, though, this should put a stop to Claude being used for vibe-coded recompilations, PC ports, and the like. Last month, for example, a Bloodborne PC port with multiplayer and keyboard-and-mouse support went viral, but its credits revealed that Claude was used in almost every aspect of the project. We've also seen AI-infested Mario Kart Wii, The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening, and Banjo-Tooie projects, just to name a few. At this point, it feels more like a rarity for the developers behind these sorts of things to declare they didn't use AI.

Hopefully, it might also reduce the number of AI-slop clones of games released on Steam. The original creator of Needle in a Haystack Simulator jokingly apologized as their game became such a hit that it spurred on numerous copycats flooding the platform, and theirs isn't the only game to see blatant recreations like this.

However, it's clearly not intended to stop people from vibe coding their own games, so I doubt we're suddenly going to see the amount of AI usage on platforms like Steam take a nosedive.

#4031. Stealth Classic Thief: The Dark Project Returns for a PS5 Remaster with New Content

One of the classics that helped create an entire genre, stealth masterpiece Thief: The Dark Project is coming to PS5 in remastered form next month, from 3rd December 2026.

This new version of the 1998 game has been remastered using Nightdive Studios' KEX Engine to produce a new edition running at 4K and 120 frames-per-second. It's got all the content of the base game, the three extra missions from Thief: Gold, and an entirely new campaign in the form of The Tarnished Mirror.

The Tarnished Mirror is a narrative bridge between The Dark Project and Thief 2: The Metal Age. In it, "a seemingly straightforward theft spirals into imprisonment, uneasy alliances and a descent into a drowned, R’lyeh-like necropolis. Players will experience an expanded enemy roster, ambitious level design and a pure Thief experience that descends into unsettling, otherworldly horror."

The bonus campaign has been created by the same people who made Thief: The Black Parade, which was a mod / expansion for Thief: Gold, made by the fans. "This collaboration marks a rare industry moment, with Nightdive and Eidos-Montréal welcoming a community creation directly into official canon," the press release added.

#4030. As devastating Xbox "reset" continues, Dishonored studio Arkane Lyon reportedly only has until November to find a new buyer before it's closed

After getting caught up in Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating layoffs and cuts earlier this year, Arkane Lyon - the beloved immersive sim studio behind the likes of Dishonored and Deathloop - reportedly only has until November to find a buyer. If the search fails, it will be shut down.

Arkane Lyon was one of a number of first-party studios reportedly facing closure ahead of Xbox's massive "reset" in July. However, when the layoffs were officially announced - bringing confirmation that 3,200 Xbox employees will eventually lose their jobs as part of the sweeping restructuring - Microsoft revealed Psychonauts developer Double Fine, State of Decay studio Undead Labs, and South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games would go independent following negotiations.

Hellblade studio Ninja Theory is now likely to close after two acquisition deals fell through, only leaving the fate of Arkane Lyon - a studio Microsoft acquired in 2021 when it purchased ZeniMax - uncertain. At the time, Xbox said it was "beginning required consultation with its Works Council to review potential strategic options" regarding Arkane, but little has been heard since.

Now, a report by French publication Le Monde (via Google Translate) has shed additional light on the studio's fate. Speaking to the publication, Printemps Écologique and the Video Game Workers’ Union (STJV) said Xbox management had informed Arkane Lyon it was facing closure on 16th July. As Le Monde notes, however, Microsoft's plan was complicated by French law, which requires a company with more than 1,000 employees to spend three months seeking a new buyer for any operational arm it plans to close. Only then, if no buyer is found, can it be shut down.

According to Le Monde, the search - alongside a consultation process and negotiations regarding an employment protection plan - began this summer, and the deadline to find a buyer for the studio is imminent, ending on 13th November. If the closure occurs, 217 workers could lose their jobs.

However, a union representative told the publication redundancy negotiations, which seemingly include efforts to get Arkane workers redeployed to other Microsoft studios, are going "badly", and that unions are trying to buy more time in the hope of saving the studio and its jobs. Reportedly, "several forms of takeover are being considered."

In response to the report, Microsoft did not confirm or deny Arkane's proposed closure, but told Le Monde, "We continue to explore various options for Arkane as part of the ongoing French consultation process". It also said it was "keeping the Social and Economic Committee and our employees informed." Internal documents seen by the publication say "the implementation of the plan [for the total and definitive cessation of the company's operations] is scheduled to begin at the end of 2026 and is expected to continue throughout the first quarter of 2027."

Amid all this turmoil, it's unclear what might happen to Arkane Lyon's current project, Marvel's Blade. In July, Xbox insisted "none of [its] first-party publicly announced games or projects" would be cancelled as part of Sharma's cuts, suggesting Blade - which hasn't been seen since its announcement in 2023 - was safe. Earlier this year, the game was rumoured to be dead, but a follow-up report from The Verge claimed that while it was "over-budget", it was now targeting a release in 2027 after an internal delay.

Earlier this month, Sharma insisted Xbox had "started to return to growth" following the company's sweeping cuts, but reports suggest three more rounds of layoffs are still to come, possibly starting before October is through.

#4029. Discord know they replaced forums, so they're making your messages in discoverable servers searchable, which immediately raises one question: what about AI?

The changes start coming into effect next month

You might want to hold off on that horny posting in your favourite discoverable Discord server. The chat service announced today that any servers that are listed as discoverable, meaning anyone can find them simply through Googling, no invite link required, will now also show messages and discussions posted in said servers on Google.

This is being done because, as Discord admits, forums aren't as popular these days. "Prior to Discord's launch, message boards were common, ranging from community-driven forums to official ones run by game studios," reads a post explaining the update. "These message boards excelled at hosting long-form, structured conversations about helping people, theory crafting, and more. While they still exist today, many have moved into Discord servers. This has led to valuable information being locked in Discord conversations, inaccessible to the wider internet. We want to fix this."

I have certainly seen this complaint myself on a number of occasions, so, to a certain degree I'm sure this will be welcome. It does immediately raise one concern for me though, that being everyone's favourite topic at the moment: AI. As it currently stands, it's Discord policy that AI companies are not allowed to train their models on a user's messages. How does this change with these messages now being publicly available? What safeguards will be put in place to prevent this, if any?

As the post explains, discoverable servers will have server web pages where messages and discussions can be found through your search engine of choice. Every discoverable server will have a server web page from November 16th, next month, but you can opt out ahead of time and once the feature is live. It's from mid-December where channel messages will be viewable on these server web pages. "Server admins decide which channels take part, and server members can choose whether their own messages appear. Usernames and avatars will not be shown alongside these messages," the post notes.

Also worth noting is that in "the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea, the member setting for Channel Messages is off by default given legal restrictions, so members’ messages won’t appear on the web unless they turn it on. Users in the teen age group are excluded completely and cannot enable Channel Messages until they’re an adult. Everywhere else, it’s on unless members turn it off."

On the one hand, sure, it'll be nice to have some of this information that was previously much harder to access publicly available. On the other, the open web is infested with corporations that are looking to harvest your data without any consequences, currently, and now something as simple as sending a Discord message could potentially aid in that. I'm glad that you have individual control over whether your own messages get seen, I just struggle to see this as an overwhelmingly positive move.

#4028. With Minecraft and Diablo shows already on the way, Netflix reportedly offered Xbox $500m for a bigger film and TV deal

A deal between Netflix and Xbox has supposedly fallen through because of one minor quibble: Netflix wanted to adapt the console maker's games for $500m, not $800m.

That's according to Puck News' Matt Belloni, who reports that Netflix offered Xbox $500m to exclusively licence the company's games and turn them into streamable films or TV shows for the next seven years.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma and the division's business affairs team then responded with an eye-watering counter offer, according to the report. Xbox supposedly asked the streamer for $800m to sign off on the same deal.

Former Netflix CCO Bela Bajaria reportedly approached the game publisher first, but the executive's departure and Xbox's expensive counter offer led to the deal falling apart. Netflix CFO Spence Neumann was apparently one of the streamer's top heads who thought the deal wasn't worth the $800m price tag.

It's unclear which games would've been included in the film and TV deal considering multiple Xbox brands are already on their way to screens both big and small. Amazon is working to adapt Wolfenstein into a live-action series and will soon debut the third season of its acclaimed Fallout show, for example, while Paramount is turning Call of Duty into a blockbuster movie.

Netflix and Xbox are still working together on other projects, though. Animated shows based on Minecraft and Diablo are already in the works, as is a live-action Gears of War film. Blizzard Entertainment president Johanna Faries recently teased the crowd at BlizzCon 2026 by suggesting Overwatch and Warcraft could receive a similar treatment, too.

"We have received record-breaking interest in our IP," Xbox said in a statement to Puck News. "Netflix is a valued partner and we are excited for the forthcoming release of our Minecraft and Diablo animated series together, among other adaptations." The outlet claims Xbox is continuing to pursue smaller licensing deals.

Game adaptations are all the rage right now. This year's excellent Resident Evil reboot, Illuminations' Super Mario Bros duology, HBO's The Last of US, Amazon's Fallout and three live-action Sonic The Hedgehog films have found huge success - and encouraged practically every major studio to go hunting for their own game licenses. They're not all hits, however. This year's Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat 2 were released to a more tepid crowd.

#4027. Monarchs at Play is a 4X strategy city-builder about chaining hexagonal tiles that only takes an hour out of your day

None of us have any bloody time any more, do we? The economy being in the toilet is obviously part of that, but the other part is that we're all adults and now we have to do responsible adult things like our laundry, and buying toilet paper, and buying toilet paper again because it simply never ends. It all makes playing games just that little bit trickier, especially when it comes to lengthy strategy game runs. If you're longing for a quick dose of some 4X strategy, though, Monarchs at Play, a turn-based city-builder that only takes an hour, might be the thing you're after.

I know that a simple hour of your time might actually be quite a lot in the greater scheme of things, but for something like a 4X strategy game, that sounds pretty reasonable to me. In Monarchs at Play, you choose from one of several monarchs, each of which has their own unique abilities and buildings. In a run, like most other city-builders, you start out small by placing what little buildings you have available to you, the ultimate goal being to place different kinds of tiles next to one another to build up combos.

Different buildings allow you to rack up resources, which in turn lets you place new buildings; you get how this works! You aren't doing this alone, however, as you have rivals to compete against, where you'll have to destroy the buildings they place to continue growing your own empire. These rivals can just be simple NPCs, but they can also be real-life players, so if you've only got an hour to spare but want to play something online, Monarchs at Play seems like it'll be a good fit.

There's a demo you can currently check out and try for yourself on Steam too. No release date attached just yet, so you'll have to keep your eyes peeled.

Judging by the official Lego site, it also feels like a reveal could be imminent

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The king kaiju seems to have woken from his slumber early, because Lego Godzilla has reportedly stomped into stores early. However, some fans aren't happy about the finished result.

According to a Reddit post from u/itsjustajoe (a prominent member of the Lego leaks community and overall reliable source), the kit was found in an undisclosed store and will apparently cost "Around $450-$500 USD." While we've obviously got to take this with a monster-sized pinch of salt, it's already been confirmed that a Lego Godzilla set was on the way. Plus, this Godzilla listing page on the Lego store seems to have just gone live – I can't find any history for it on Wayback Machine, which implies it's new. This, combined with the kit's appearance in-store, suggests an announcement is imminent.

Unfortunately, the community isn't celebrating just yet; some fans on the Reddit thread are already crossing their fingers that it isn't real. "This has to be fake… surely 😭😭😭," writes Latter-Macaron-2575 with over 600 upvotes. "Part of me hopes it is fake, another part hopes it isnt so i can save my money," agrees Daniel_Spidey.

Another monster set just dropped that has been going over well – Lego Dragon Ball Shenron & Goku from the Lego Store has been creating waves of a good kind, That's just as well, because it promises to be "just the beginning" for the range.

Personally, I'm gonna go against the grain and say that I quite like the big guy. I'd prefer a good look at his face before passing final judgement, but to me, it captures the scale and grandeur of Godzilla – and those almost-glowing blue spines look fantastic. My one quibble is the pose; I think the original submission (this is an 'Ideas' kit, which means it's based on a design made by the community) was truer to the iconic kaiju, capturing his weight and gait. It's possible that this less-hunched design was based on the original Toho design or the new Minus One equivalent rather than the Monsterverse version, but it's unclear. It could even be an amalgamation of all the above, hence why it looks a little different.

Because Lego often announces new sets in the first half of the week, I'd keep a very close eye out – with the listing page for the Ideas project now live, I wouldn't be surprised to see an official unveiling later today or tomorrow. What with the rumored release date being November 27th (making it one of the latest new Lego sets in November), that kind of lead-in would make sense.

Until then, what do you think of the kit? Shout about it in the comments.

So far as other fan-submitted designs go, a Star Wars game dev creates a Lego Biddy Blas model you can build at home. It's not official, but it could give some of the best Lego sets a run for their money in terms of creativity.

#4025. Travis Touchdown 'Will Definitely Be Back' for No More Heroes 20th Anniversary

Goichi Suda (aka Suda51), head honcho of developer Grasshopper Manufacture, has given fans fresh hope of more to come for the cult favourite No More Heroes series.

Speaking to Famitsu as part of a wider interview, he's asked about No More Heroes as it's approaching its 20th anniversary in 2027.

Asked if there's anything being planned for the occasion, Suda51 says his team and publisher Marvelous are indeed cooking up something. (Quotations machine translated.)

"Marvelous is aware of this, so we definitely want to do something together for the 20th anniversary," he says. "We're planning to deliver something special, so please look forward to it. Travis Touchdown will definitely be back!"

He didn't provide any further details, but it sounds like there's something for fans to look forward to in the new year.

The original No More Heroes was released in Japan in December 2007, and was later brought to western audiences in 2008.

There have been several games in the series, with the latest being No More Heroes 3, released for PS5 and PS4 in 2022.

Anyway, there's not a lot to go on here, but it seems fans of the franchise have got something to look forward to in the near future.

Are you excited to see what Suda51 has planned for No More Heroes' 20th anniversary? Tell us in the comments section below.

#4024. Feature: 25 Years Later, How Many Of These Original Xbox Launch Titles Have You Played?

From the original North American launch on November 15, 2001

Welcome to the month of Xbox's 25th anniversary! Xbox will be celebrating that milestone officially on November 15th, but before we get there, we thought we'd use the chance to highlight the very first games that ever launched on Xbox.

To do that, we're going back to the initial list of North American Xbox launch titles, of which there were 20 in all. Some of them are obvious standouts, such as Halo: Combat Evolved, Fuzion Frenzy, Dead or Alive 3 and Project Gotham Racing, while others are more obscure - Arctic Thunder, Dark Summit, Mad Dash Racing, etc.

Here's the full list of all 20 launch titles:

Now, of course, some of these games are still playable to this day on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, while others have always remained locked to the original Xbox. The likes of Project Gotham Racing, Shrek and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2x are highly-requested additions to the Xbox backwards compatibility library, but it seems unlikely they'll ever make the cut at this point - almost certainly due to licensing reasons.

However, you may not know that games like Cel Damage and Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee are still playable to this day on modern consoles, and they're still well worth checking out despite their age.

So, how many of these original Xbox launch titles have you played? Let us know down in the comments section below, and please do give us your recommendations with some of the obscure ones - NHL Hitz is still one of my faves!

#4023. Nintendo's Shigeru Miyamoto says even if gen-AI "were to eventually handle everything, there will always be a role left" for human designers

Legendary Nintendo developer Shigeru Miyamoto - who led development on classic games such as Super Mario 64 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time - has argued that the rise of generative AI tools won't necessarily replace human talent.

Next month, Shigeru Miyamoto will become the first ever video game developer to be awarded the Order of Culture by the Emperor of Japan, a hugely prestigious honour. But in a recent press conference dedicated to the award, he also shared some thoughts about gen-AI and its use in game production.

"Our generation lived through a period of rapid computer development - a time when tools were constantly evolving, moving from typewriters to word processors,” he said while speaking to the press, in quotes translated by VGC. Miyamoto argued that a designer's true capabilities "finally came to the fore" as technology advanced and was capable of handling more of what might be considered "labor", and a similar transition may take place with generative AI tech.

"While the act of creation is inherently satisfying, there's a danger: one might find satisfaction in the labor itself and mistakenly believe that a high-quality piece of work has been created," he added. If generative-AI software replaces more tasks involved in game production, human game devs might have "an opportunity to reflect on what's really important."

"Looking back at past designs, there are some that were created merely by copying and pasting. Yet, such work rarely stands the test of time; it lacks the individual’s particular design intention," Miyamoto continued. "Because the process relies on an individual's intent, with the computer serving as an assistant for the labor, I believe that even as technology continues to evolve, and even if AI were to eventually handle everything, there will always be a role left for us to play."

Masahiro Sakurai was a bit less optimistic about a potentially AI-first future than his peer. The Smash Bros. director recently said gen-AI tech might lead to a surge of unoriginal and unprofitable games, though it won't be able to replicate the creativity of humans.

Nintendo itself hasn't outright ruled out the possibility of using gen-AI tools in the future, but former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser assured folks that the company's games would retain a "human touch" last year. "We still believe that what makes our games special is our developers, their artistic capabilities, their insight into how people play," Bowser said at the time.

Nintendo is somewhat at odds with several of its contemporaries when it comes to AI adoption, however. Square Enix CEO Takashi Kiryu previously said the company would be "aggressive in applying AI." Sega, Capcom, Level-5, Epic Games and a number of other high-profile game studios have admitted to using gen-AI in some form, as well. Xbox even opened an entire division seemingly dedicated to experimenting with the tech.

#4022. Part idle game, part automation game, Moon Sweepers exploits the sickness in me that adores both Satisfactory and Cookie Clicker

In space, no one can hear you have an existential crisis

When Edwin talked about Moon Sweepers yesterday he focused on the artisanal approach to space rock cleaning. Like the puritan he is, he wants to wipe away all the dust on the moon using a toothbrush. He says you should take pride in your work, stick one spacesuit-clad middle finger up to the machines and say 'Fuck off, robots. Let me show you my art!" as you get down on all fours and brush away moon dust.

I mean, sure, when I first created a new game in Moon Sweepers, I painted with my toothbrush:

But then I got down to the serious business of trying to clean up the dusty moon, section by section and all thoughts of art left my head.

When you first begin Moon Sweepers, you're faced with an entire planetoid broken down into hexagonal tiles, each deep with dust and needing a brushing. The first sectors you'll clean take an age to clear. The toothbrush only carves a thin groove into the dirt and the tile is comparatively vast. Your backpack fills with hoovered up dust as you clean and when it's filled you need to head back to base to sell it off. Each kilo sold nets you a single dollar, but with that cash you can buy improved tools, swapping your toothbrush for a hand brush, and eventually for a broom.

It was only after I bought my broom I realised – too late to save myself – that I was playing an incremental game.

Moon Sweepers is an incremental game. There are sectors of dusty moon as far as the eye can see. The tools you start with a small, but they grow in potency, with increasingly large brooms that can be upgraded with wider brush heads and larger backpacks, meaning you can collect moon matter for longer before heading back to base to cash it in. But Moon Sweepers is also an automation game, and it's only when I clocked that that I realised I was truly done for.

Once you buy a hammer from your base's shop, you can start building conveyor belts, space dust processing plants, and robot vacuums. Stretch a conveyor out from your base to one of the sectors of the moon you're clearing and you can dump filled dust canisters on the belt instead of heading home to sell it. The conveyor whisks away the dust-filled tube and sells it for you, letting you spend longer in the fields scrubbing. Pour dust into a processing plant and it will compact it into a more valuable resource, earning you extra cash for your labour. And, well, robot vacuum cleaners look like NASA-branded Roombas. They clear the dust from a wide grid around their docking station.

Moon Sweepers, this incremental game in Satisfactory's clothing, now has me thinking I can genuinely clean the entire moon. I've abandoned Edwin's artful approach to the task and I am all in on using the robots, conveyor belts, and moon rovers to complete the job. I somehow believe this even though I have only so far cleaned 19 sectors and, according to the handbook, there are 163,842 in total. I believe this despite Steam reviews from players with many more hours under their belts shouting to me that this is a futile task. "We are 10 hours in and we are already maxed out on all the latest tools and vehicles and we are not even 1% done with cleaning," writes Marten. "20 hours played, just reached 1% of surface cleared," says Bim Fimberdim. "After 26 Hours I cleared 1.6% of the moon," writes Amigos_Of_Bako.

Maybe it's the ease and definition of progress, which is so unlike life. The irony of getting this fixated on Moon Sweepers is that I'm currently doing a lot of DIY in my flat and, despite resembling the manual labour in some of these games, it has none of the simplicity.

I went into this past weekend meaning to end it with a painted living room with some new alive bookshelves. I had to measure the alcove for some shelves, drill the holes for the brackets, cut the shelves to size, clean everything up, and then paint the living room. Yet, at the end of the weekend, I had fewer shelves and less paint on the walls than when I started. Delay after delay, complication after complication, and setback after setback meant that progress was slow and, when it did game, was more like a ship tacking against the wind than a straight line. What could have been a fulfilling, satisfying task, was infuriating and stressful.

Perhaps, right now, I want to clean up the moon because sweeping all of its 163,842 sections somehow feels more attainable and realistic than fitting these bookshelves.

#4021. Until Dawn 2 to Showcase New PS5 Gameplay and More in Alamo Drafthouse Livestream

Sony is getting the ball rolling on Until Dawn 2, its narrative horror adventure game making its debut in a few short months.

The PS5 exclusive title, developed by Firesprite, launches on 28th January 2027, but you can get a good look at the game before then, as the company plans to show it off in a fancy live event this December.

Until Dawn 2 will be making a special appearance at American cinema chain Alamo Drafthouse (which Sony Pictures owns, by the way) on 11th December, 2026, where attendees will be able to see "an exclusive gameplay showcase" as well as enjoy a horror movie marathon.

The event will also include "special talent appearances", presumably meaning that actors from the game will be showing up live.

If you're unable to get to an Alamo Drafthouse, the gameplay showcase will be available to watch via livestream so you can catch a glimpse of the new game in action. More details are coming soon.

While it's a sequel to the very successful original game, Until Dawn 2 focuses on a brand new cast and entirely different story.

It features a group of ghost hunters that travel to a remote island, having been offered a TV deal to document its mysterious abandoned resort.

The new premise and characters aside, this is very much in the same mould as the first Until Dawn; you follow this group of people and must make choices along the way that can have a serious impact on the story.

Heavily inspired by horror cinema, this event makes a lot of sense.

Sony has been quietly building interest in Until Dawn 2 by introducing each character one at a time. There's now a little under three months to go before this is in our hands, so I expect we'll be seeing plenty more as we get closer.

#4020. Leaked Mass Effect 5 trailer is being "re-scored" by one of the original trilogy's composers, so folks can get a taste of his musical vision for the game

One of the composers who contributed to the scores of the original Mass Effect trilogy has decided to re-soundtrack the Mass Effect Universe trailer which leaked following the game's cancellation and BioWare's closure. Sam Hulick's aim, aside from making this year's N7 Day a tiny bit less depressing if he can deliver as planned, is to share some of his "musical vision" for the RPG.

Hulick announced his plan on BlueSky, having already started working on a new score for the trailer "for no reason other than closure". "My plan is to release the re-scored Mass Effect Universe trailer for N7 Day," he wrote. "A little tight, since I'm a bit busy pitching for a new game, but I'll see what I can do! I don't wanna rush it, and I want it to properly represent my musical vision for MEU."

With composer Austin Wintory having recently released a collection of tunes he put together while in talks to potentially work on a proper soundtrack for what would have been the fifth Mass Effect game, Hulick's efforts will mean there are two different takes on what Universe might've sounded like out there in the wild. It's somewhat of a silver lining to the dark cloud of the game's demise. You can rightly argue that any canned game tends to be eulogised in terms that point to it having had the potential to be the best thing since sliced bread in a fashion that perhaps over-eggs the pudding a bit, but it's always interesting to learn what those who did or could have worked on such games had in mind.

Having takes on Universe's soundtrack from both Hulick and Wintory out there certainly isn't hurting anyone. The former's also offered his view on the ongoing community-driven efforts to pressure EA into not putting the series on ice, as they have the likes of Burnout in the past. "What really sucks & cannot be undone is all the folks at BioWare who lost their jobs," he wrote. "Even if EA licensed the IP, that doesn't solve anything for them. Someone with a lotta cash would have to license it AND hire the team."

Pending that sort of miracle, the likes of the trailer, these tunes, and other details ex-BioWare devs have shared about what the studio hoped to achieve with Universe are at least meaning fans aren't entirely left in the dark about the work going on during BioWare's final chapter.

#4019. Xbox's first chief operating officer Helen Chiang leaves Microsoft just three months into the job

UPDATE: Xbox responds, and source familiar with the situation alleges Chiang was terminated for "policy violations".

UPDATE 6.00pm (UK): In a formal statement, Xbox told Eurogamer: "We don't discuss individual personnel matters. We're grateful for Helen's years of service and wish her well".

A verified source familiar with the situation separately told Eurogamer that Helen Chiang had allegedly been "terminated for policy violations". Eurogamer has not been able to independently verify this claim.

Eurogamer has contacted Helen Chiang for comment.

ORIGINAL STORY 2.00pm BST: Helen Chiang, Xbox's first-ever chief operating officer (COO), is leaving Microsoft just three months after taking the job.

According to The Verge, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed Chiang's departure in an internal memo circulated on 23rd October.

"Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I'm grateful for her years of service and wish her well," Sharma wrote.

Sharma provided no details on why Chiang - who'd been at Microsoft for 21 years and had previously served as head of Minecraft - was leaving the company, only adding, "we'll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalised". It's thought her duties will be shared between other Xbox execs.

Sharma created the role in July as part of Xbox's massive "reset", saying it was needed to "work toward a shared goal, make the right tradeoffs, and get things done". It also came with 3200 layoffs and four studio departures in "most significant" Xbox restructuring in history.

Microsoft revealed that Psychonauts developer Double Fine, State of Decay studio Undead Labs, and South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games would go independent following negotiations, while Hellblade developer Ninja Theory is now likely to close after two acquisition deals fell through.

Arkane Lyon - the beloved immersive sim studio behind the likes of Dishonored and Deathloop - is the one still in limbo, and yesterday we learned it reportedly only has until November to find a buyer.

Clearly Donnie Yen should be in more games

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The people love a good action RPG. At least that's what the numbers around the launch of Phantom Blade Zero would indicate, since it's managed to shift millions of copies and attract north of 820,000 concurrent players on Steam in its first weekend.

Developer and publisher S-Game shared one of these stats on social media, posting a nice big graphic on Twitter announcing that Phantom Blade Zero crossed the four million mark in copies sold in just three days. An impressive turnaround by any metric.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support!" reads the caption. The image notes the Metacritic score of 88 and the Steam review score of 89%. Not too shabby whatsoever.

Phantom Blade Zero has sold over 4 million copies in just 72 hours!🔥 Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support! https://t.co/XPhq14v9YNNovember 2, 2026

Speaking of Valve's store, a healthy amount of these players are jumping into the Phantom World on PC. On Steam Charts, the peak concurrent player count sits at 822,361. That immediately places the release among the most popular games currently on the store, outstripping the all-time records of Marvel Rivals and Battlefield 6, and even the 24-hour peaks of stalwarts like PUBG and the omni-present Bongo Cat.

At time of writing, nearly 400,000 are playing on the PC marketplace. A healthy, robust audience was ready and waiting for this game, it seems.

Drawing on wuxia, a genre of Chinese storytelling that fuses martial arts and fantasy elements, Phantom Blade Zero involves you trying to help an assassin clear his name after he's framed for a murder by the organization he works for. The history Chinese setting looks gorgeous and the martial arts-infused combat seems like a tonne of fun.

Donnie Yen is involved, and part of me likes to think he's a driving force behind the emphatic playerbase. We're unlikely to ever get an Ip Man game, but we have this, and it's close enough, in all honesty.

#4017. OG Xbox Game 'Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee' Gets Remastered, But What Do The Critics Think?

Was it worth digging the original Xbox title back up?

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee launched on the original Xbox in 2003, a few months after its GameCube debut, and sadly, only in North America. The kaiju arena-brawler, which depicted the iconic King of Monsters, Godzilla, body-slamming Ghidorah into various cityscapes, has apparently made a big enough impact to warrant Atari funding a remaster in 2026.

Sadly, the whole North American release made it quite difficult for us Brits to get our mucky mitts on the game, and DAMM wasn't a big enough deal for Xbox to share the game with the rest of the world. DAMM did get the backward compatibility treatment, however, only on Xbox 360, and again restricted to North America.

I guess then, we're quite pleased Atari decided to take a punt on a DAMM remaster. Even though it seems to share many of the original's downfalls, Godzilla's WWE antics are going to be available on November 3rd on Xbox Series X|S, and best of all, I can play it from my lovely little home in Cornwall.

So, here's what the critics are saying about Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered:

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered brings the classic kaiju brawler roaring back with impressive rebuilt visuals, satisfying arena destruction, and chaotic multiplayer battles. While its limited roster and tedious character unlocks feel dated, the accessible combat and faithful Godzilla presentation make this a thoroughly entertaining return for the King of the Monsters."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered feels like a new game with its graphical upgrade, held back slightly by a lack of any other meaningful new additions and a somewhat grindy gameplay loop."

"Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a satisfyingly faithful update to a beloved Kaiju brawler. It’s simple and fun, with local and online multiplayer keeping you around for the long haul despite a wafer-thin single-player experience. Now if we could just get a remaster of Save The Earth and Unleashed."

Review Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (Switch 2) - The King Returns With A Fun But Thin Kaiju Brawler

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is at its best when it simulates the idea of smashing kaiju toys together as a kid in short sessions with friends, and at its worst when it attempts to prolong a game that never had much depth to begin with. The result is a remaster I’m glad exists considering the drought of Godzilla brawlers, but with a few caveats–not to mention the sting of realizing that the original GameCube and Xbox game were absent of arbitrary grinding."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered remains goofy fun, and Atari’s remaster looks and runs well. It’s still a rather simple game and probably not the most comprehensive when it comes to the characters and lore. But it’s a good time and offers quite a few different modes to get acclimated and beat up famous faces."

"Right now, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a great version of a good retro game. Because the game was remade from the ground up, I wish the developers had made a super version of the Godzilla trilogy with more content. While Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered’s combat is really fun, there’s not much depth. There are lots of modes, and a bit of RPG unlocking, but this isn’t a deep fighting game that’s going to be played at tournaments. It’s a great budget buy for Godzilla fans. But more content would have made Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered a more obvious recommendation. If you’re at all curious, or have any fondness for the original game, it remains a fun time."

"In the media shadow of sacred monsters like Grand Theft Auto VI and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, only an equally fearless monstrosity could face them: Godzilla. Nearly a quarter century after its release on GameCube, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee returns with a remaster that discreetly refreshes the audiovisual experience and improves the progression without betraying its structure. The core is that of a 3D fighting game in which kaiju clashes are accompanied by the destruction of entire cities, in a blaze of explosions and particle effects. Behind this chaos lies a combat system that's immediate, but not always precise and balanced, suspended somewhere between classic fighting games and the festive jumble of a party game. The mechanics are simple, despite a certain unwieldiness in the movements, and the best of the action is found especially in local multiplayer."

Well, there you have it, folks! Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is an almost perfect example of a good '7' rated game. At the time of writing, the remaster is holding down a 72 score on Metacritic.

What's interesting is that the original Xbox release scored 73 on Metacritic - a single point higher than the remaster. It's funny how 23 years can pass and a game can be reviewed almost identically.

#4016. Prime Video's Fallout reality competition Fallout Shelter: The Experiment premieres in January

Prime Video's Fallout reality competition, Fallout Shelter: The Experiment, will premiere on 13th January 2027.

According to Prime Video's announcement on Fallout Day, 23rd October, the first four episodes will arrive on launch day, with the rest following weekly. It will be available in more than 240 countries and territories.

The unscripted series sees everyday participants test their aptitude for the apocalypse inside Vault-Tec's bomb-proof vault shelters, facing head-to-head drills, psychological dilemmas, and morally challenging trials. The one "dweller" who emerges as the winner will take home $1m.

"The world is ending," a short cinematic teases. "The competition is just beginning." It then cuts to "Fallout Shelter: The Experiment."

Good morning, future Vault Dwellers! Please Stand By for an important announcement. Fallout Shelter: The Experiment — an all-new competition series — arrives January 13, only on @primevideo. pic.twitter.com/U87TSfNayV

It's produced by Studio Lambert - the company behind The Traitors, The Circle, and Squid Game: The Challenge - in co-production with Kilter Films, the production company of Fallout TV series creators Jonathan Nolan and Lisa Joy.

Bethesda Game Studios is involved in association, with Todd Howard and James Altman among the executive producers.

#4015. "Creation without a creator": Pathologic 3's devs have refused to patch an invisible apple tree, and for a blissful moment, I thought they were lying to poison Google's AI

"Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something."

Magnificent, depressing plague colony fable Pathologic 3 has received a sizeable game update that adds some new difficulty modes, a photo feature, and some new, worryingly folkloric methods of defeating a murky embodiment of disease. Developers Ice Pick Lodge have also staunchly refused to remove an invisible apple tree, describing this apparently "famous" bug as a hallmark of a game whose "symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product". This appears to be the last major update for Pathologic 3, so that invisible apple tree is staying in the game forever.

I confess, when I first read the Steam blog in question, I doubted. The thing about invisible apple trees is that they are quite easy to confuse with apple trees that are simply not there. Pathologic in general is a house of lies: as Quintin Smith (RPS in peace) put it in his legendary Butchering Pathologic trilogy, "absolutely everybody has an angle, everyone's bending the truth and trying to twist you round their fingers." Pathologic 3 especially is a purgatorial time travel story that must be continually rewritten, a crock of festering rumours enclosed by an enormous, phantom theatre. As such, I read Ice-Pick's typically professorial account of the "invisible apple tree" with intense suspicion.

"Roger Ebert, the famous film critic, once argued that video games could never be art," the devs write on Steam. "It's curious, then, that urinals and bottle racks achieved that status with hardly any struggle, thanks to Marcel Duchamp. So Myst, StarCraft, or Pathologic can't be art, but a urinal can? The distinction, perhaps, lies in function. A urinal placed in a museum stops being plumbing and becomes a symbol. A video game, on the other hand, remains a functional object. We still have to use it.

"But enough about urinals," they go on. "Let's turn to another famous work: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs. In this work, a chair is no longer simply something to sit on. Whether it's comfortable hardly matters: as a work of art, it still functions. A video game can also become a symbolic chair. But you still have to sit on it. There's a running joke that Pathologic is a great game that nobody actually plays. Somehow, it really has become something like Kosuth's symbolic chair, one nobody is obliged to sit on. Which raises a question: should we even fix Pathologic if its symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product?

"Take visual bugs, for instance. Are they broken chairs you can't sit on, or artistic decisions?" Ice-Pick continue. "Consider our famous invisible apple tree. Oh, apple tree! Why are you here? What are we supposed to do with you? This is probably the most famous bug in Pathologic 3. We've received more complaints about it than almost anything else. We have to admit there were moments when we genuinely hated that tree. Are we going to fix it in this update? Perhaps not.

"After all, it's a creation of the machine," they conclude. "Somehow, the game's code produced this impossible object. And over time, our annoyance at it has begun to turn into a strange affection. Sometimes an artistic act lies not in creating something, but in the artist's decision about it. Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something. So the tree stays."

Aside from making me pine for a world in which, say, EA add a "hypernormalisation" slider to The Sims, or Ubisoft redefine Assassin's Creed parkour as a Situationist dérive (yes, I too have read books), the blog post filled me with confusion. I couldn't remember any invisible apple trees in Pathologic 3. I also couldn't find any English language mention of Pathologic 3's avowedly "famous" ethereal vegetation on Google or the Steam forums, save for in stories covering the game's latest update.

My weakness for talk of symbolism notwithstanding, I began to worry that Ice-Pick might be winding us up. And by "us", I specifically mean pathetic videogame reporters, hunting for a cool bug anecdote to wrap a headline around. Pathetic videogame reporters who are subject to the wiles of Google Search, which has recently become an AI-driven abomination that subsumes and rewords all knowledge while starving actual information sources of traffic.

There have been efforts to screw with Google's AI summaries, planting nonsense on Reddit and elsewhere in the hope of skewing or outright sabotaging the chatbot's datasets. Perhaps Pathologic 3's "invisible apple tree" was one such poison apple, I mused to myself, offered to Gemini in the manner of a cackling forest hag thrusting suspiciously plump and juicy fruit at cherubic village children. Associations foamed in my brain: Ice-Pick Lodge are based in Kazakhstan... where apples first grew in the wild. Breathless, I contacted Ice-Pick Lodge for a clarification, and – bah, it turns out there is an invisible apple tree in Pathologic 3, after all.

"The slightly longer story goes like this," producer Alexander Souslov told me over DM. "At some point (nobody remembers exactly when), one of our tree assets - an apple tree, to be precise - started rendering incorrectly and became invisible. The leaves were still there, but the trunk was gone. We tried to fix it, but ran into the classic game developer's dilemma: is this really important enough to spend resources on, rather than, say, making another cutscene or putting together another quest?"

Souslov says the apple tree drove him "absolutely nuts". (I feel like he could have rolled with some line about "one bad apple spoiling the barrel", but hey, I'm not one of those stuffed shirts over at Edge Magazine - I don't mind interviewees mixing their arboreal metaphors.) Eventually, however, he made peace with the exasperatingly trunkless tree. "I started thinking: wait a minute, this thing basically came into existence all by itself. Do I really have to fix it?

"And that's when I remembered Marcel Duchamp and his ideas, and suddenly I began to feel that we'd accidentally created something beautiful," Souslov went on. "Invisible trees next to the Cathedral, where time flows in different directions. There's a strange kind of beauty in that, in the very act of creation without a creator.

"So I made an executive artistic decision: we're keeping the tree, and we're officially declaring it part of the world. So no pranks involved! Just a happy accident elevated to the status of artistic intent."

With Souslov's guidance, I fired up an old Pathologic 3 save and tracked down the invisible apple tree in-game, right next to the aforesaid Cathedral. Please find a picture of the thing's spectral foliage below – poetically captured by moonlight at the dead of 1am, through a fog of in-game Apathy. I also belatedly checked Reddit, and yep, there's a paper trail, though Souslov added that the bug is inconsistent: "their whimsical behavior makes it even better as an artistic expression - the apple tree may decide it won't meet with you today."

I remain compelled by the idea of developers telling dirty great porkies in their patchnotes, if only to excite and upset games journalists who really don't have this much time to spare. Mojang used to do that thing with Herobrine, remember?

Given the escalating chatbotification of everything, I think we are entering an exhilarating new age of lying on the internet, in which deceit and doublespeak have become weapons of resistance against the algorithm. But I also just think videogames and their creators are often more fun when they are two-faced, providing there's some fundamental benevolence involved. Videogames are all about sleight of hand, and devs should take more pleasure in that. Thank you to Pathologic 3 for planting this seed.
