#3918. As Skydance merges with Warner Bros. and Paramount, the company offers voluntary redundancy and mandates return to the office

Skydance - the newly formed corporate megazord combining Warner Bros and Paramount - has issued a full five-day return-to-office mandate to employees, and offered voluntary buyouts as the merging of the companies begins.

The company was formed earlier this month following a much-debated $110bn Paramount acquisition of Warner Bros., in which both companies were squished together to be led by a refreshed board, which includes former UK prime minister Tony Blair (in an advisory role), philanthropist Laurene Powell, and former Activision CEO Bobby Kotick.

In an internal email seen by Vertical Slice, CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz told employees that in-person collaboration is "vital" for the company going forward.

"Especially in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room, sharing perspectives, challenging one another and solving problems," the email read. "Being together isn't just about showing up. It's about inspiring one another, learning and coaching, forming friendships and having access to the casual conversations that spark something great.

"With that in mind, we will adopt a five-day in-office policy across all of Skydance. We truly believe this is in the best interest of our company and our people. We've seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them."

The voluntary buyouts, meanwhile - which for those who don't know is an opportunity for employees to leave the company with a severance package - were described as a "one time offer", though it was not clear which teams within Skydance are eligible to accept it.

Skydance now includes the gaming studios once under Paramount and Warner Bros. This includes the game studios Netherrealm (Mortal Kombat), Portkey Games (Hogwarts Legacy), Avalanche Software (not to be confused with Avalanche Studios), Paramount Games Studios, and various other WB studios. It is unclear whether developers at these studios have been offered the voluntary buyout, nor when their employees will have to return to the office.

Skydance is not the only company to have offered voluntary buyouts recently. This week Microsoft offered 60,000 of its employees the same deal - that's roughly 25 percent of its staff - amid sweeping Xbox layoffs and its big AI push. Last year, EA also introduced a return-to-office policy to its employees, with its CEO saying in-person work creates "a kinetic energy that fuels creativity."

#3917. Wooshy wuxia actioner Phantom Blade Zero is sharp enough on the Steam Machine, if blunted on the Steam Deck

It would appear that Phantom Blade Zero (Phantom Blade 0? Zero? Let’s go with Zero) demanding more gigs than a mismanaged stadium is doing little to stop people playing the thing. It therefore stands to reason at least some folks will want to run S-Game Studio’s lightly Soulsy sword-em-up on the Steam Machine, so let us now examine how said GabeCube stands up to its effects-heavy martial artistry. With some settings proposals, natch.

Two signs boded poorly, before I got to testing the Machine. The first was a comment on Oisin’s day one patch piece, warning of heavy glitching on a Linux system. The second was my Steam Deck OLED, also a Linux system, being incapable of running Phantom Blade Zero at even close to a steady 30fps; even with the Low preset and some nasty-looking Ultra Performance upscaling, the game’s flashy moves and jerking (apologies – cinematic) camera shifts made for regular framerate drops into the teens.

Fortunately, the Steam Machine is much more resilient, even if it does benefit from a few quality cuts (and, realistically, will struggle if pushed beyond standard 1080p.) The Medium preset and Quality-level FSR are enough for 45-60fps in what I’ve played so far, and the High preset – while a touch susceptible to sub-40fps dips for my liking – is at least playable without major bugs or stuttering.

Strangely enough, the only major technical problem I’ve had wasn’t caused by graphics, or the Linux-based SteamOS, but the Steam Controller I was playing with. Despite being assured during the boot process that I was being treated to the Official Gamepad Configuration – cor! – an unresponsive map-opening button left me immobile during a prompt tutorial. Immobile and, I suppose without a map, lost. It turns out this this is a common bug with the Steam Controller specifically, and can be fixed by remapping the Select button, in SteamOS’s controller settings, to emulate the effect of clicking the touchpad of a PS5 pad. PC gaming.

With that sorted, Phantom Blade Zero seems to work fine? If I was nitpicking I’d point out that some high-drama sequences are visibly less buttery than the slower, roaming sections, which can exceed 60fps on Medium. Same for a lot of cutscenes, which aren’t hard-locked to 30fps like prerendered scenes often are, but do cause heavy framerate drops for little apparent reason. Still, it’s reasonable when actually playing.

Settings-wise, that Medium preset (with FSR on Quality) works well if you’re lazy. But a few of Phantom Blade Zero’s individual quality options aren’t terribly performance-sapping by themselves, and than thus be tuned upwards for a slightly nicer-looking wuxia tale with minimal drawback. Have a crack with the following:

Don’t miss those Dynamic Resolution Quality and Super Resolution Output Scale tweaks; on their defaults, they both make the game uglier than it needs to be. And on the subject of Super Resolution, FSR upscaling does leave a bit of roughness on certain edges, but then at 1080p, so does FSR even when it’s on its Native Resolution setting. You might as well get the extra frames.

Yoshida says the divisive expansion's sluggish pace "shows shortcomings on my part as the director," which seems a tad harsh

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Final Fantasy 14 producer and director Naoki "Yoshi-P" Yoshida knows one of Dawntrail's biggest issues at launch was the story's pacing, so the team is putting in the work to ensure that Evercold doesn't suffer the same fate.

Speaking to the media at Final Fantasy 14's Japanese leg of Fan Fest, Yoshida takes a question about what the team behind the MMO has learned from Dawntrail and how important it has been for Evercold's development.

"This time we are putting in serious consideration on the sense of tempo," Yoshida says, per a mod from the Final Fantasy 14 subreddit who was in attendance. "Back at Dawntrail we were being really careful in depicting new lands, new cultures, new encounters and this greatly slowed down the pacing on story progression. The fact that this did not align with players’ motivation of 'keep moving forward' shows shortcomings on my part as the director."

To remedy the pacing issues for Evercold, Yoshida says the team is moving some of the aforementioned focus to side quests, meaning you can enjoy that kind of thing if and when you want.

"This is actually connected to Final Fantasy 14's overall evolution, so we have to consider how precious players' time they have here," Yoshida adds. "After all, we will face the fact on how it's difficult for this to be relatable to players if the story doesn't progress at a brisk, fast-paced tempo, therefore we are placing a strong emphasis on this aspect this time."

I have been cautiously optimistic about Evercold since it was unveiled early this year, and this is another step in the right direction. While Dawntrail's story does eventually get good – doubly so in the post-expansion patches – it puts you in the position of having to defend it by telling your raid-brained pals to "stick with it, honestly," which is not an amazing place to be in games or other media like TV or film.

Dawntrail had other issues, sure, though Square Enix has shown enough consideration about that elsewhere. Of course, how this all works will remain to be seen. I've played Final Fantasy 14 for a long ol' time, and I've seen expansions launch with pacing issues – looking at you, Stormblood – that were remedied in later expansions. Hopefully Evercold sticks the landing in a way that hangs around for many expansions after.

#3914. As No Man's Sky arrives on mobile, Hello Games celebrates with a spooky update for all that includes delivery missions and "seamless" interstellar travel

Today's the day iPhone and iPad owners finally get to boldly go into No Man's Sky's procedurally generated universe, adding two more devices to the game's already long list of compatible platforms. But developer Hello Games isn't stopping there. It's also launching a new update, Forsaken, for all players, bringing a bit of seasonal spookiness to the exploratory space sim.

With No Man's Sky's big tenth anniversary update now out in the wild and its associated limited-time expedition over, Hello Games is taking players to what it calls the "darker side of the universe" this Halloween. Here, we're told, enigmatic traders are gathering in search of strange samples - ranging from haunted tech to biological horrors - and it's up to players to step out in search of them. That means dives into No Man's Sky's creepier corners, including derelict hulks, abandoned freighters, and infested outposts.

In return for their labours, players can acquire new seasonally themed shipbuilding options - leaning into the "creepy and organic side of sleek". These include biomechanical corvette modules, new cockpits, and a new interior set "inspired by a distant galaxy". Additionally there are new weapon and space suit styles: the larva tank helmet and wriggling grub cannon multi-tool. Hello Games' pre-release press material is a bit vague on whether this is all limited time stuff - perhaps in the form of a new Expedition - but there's also mention of "new features and gameplay" that sounds a little more permanent.

For instance, there’s talk of new postal missions - which see players "becoming a delivery driver across the galaxy" - alongside UI tweaks, including a radial menu for weapon selection, a new minimal HUD mode, and "dozens" of accessibility additions. The studio has also added what it calls "seamless warping", meaning you can just lock onto the brightest star in the sky and travel straight there without visiting the galactic map.

So that's the Forsaken update, which is available today on Mac, PC, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Switch 1 & 2, Xbox One, Xbox Series X/S, VR, and - as now - iPhone and iPad. No Man's Sky is said to work with iPhone 11 and above, as well as 3rd Generation iPad Air and above, with the first bit of the exploratory space sim available to try for free. Mobile players can expect custom touch controls, all 40+ previously released updates, and a svelte 4GB download size.

So there you go! Full patch notes for No Man's Sky's Forsaken update can be found on Hello Games' website. And if you're in the mood for a bit more related reading, Eurogamer recently spoke to the No Man's Sky players building utopia at the end of the universe - and it's a fascinating story.

#3913. Warframe's fantasy-pilled sister Soulframe finally goes open to all this November, though Digital Extremes are "nervous" about certain changes

They're celebrating the end of closed alpha by poisoning the world

Warframe creators Digital Extremes have announced that their free-to-play fantasy RPG Soulframe will be available for everyone to download on 6th November, after two years in closed alpha. Finally, you serfs without "prelude" keys will be able to fire up Soulframe.com and make sense of my ranting about the sleeping animals on the lobby screen.

The new "open prelude" will land shortly before the game's 17th major update, Verse of the Veilands, which lets you grow your Omen wolfpup allies into rideable adult wolves by finding the ingredients for a special biscuit. More importantly, prelude 17 violently rearranges the game's wistful world, adding an Ubisoft-esque region purging system that is designed to guide new players a bit more emphatically towards the game's "votives". Aka, missions. Yes, Digital Extremes sort of have a bespoke term for every game feature in Soulframe. I find this can be either charming or maddening, depending on how much sleep I've had.

Here's how the region purging will work: after completing the game's Tormented Stag quest, you'll find that the landscape is being corrupted by siphons deployed by the villainous star-faring Ode faction. You have to complete votives to build energy and learn the sacred song of each region, allowing you to cleanse it and restore the environment.

In a roundtable preview session last week, creative director Geoff Crookes and lead designer Scott McGregor expressed a certain amount of anxiety about deliberately polluting Soulframe's fairytale ambience. "Scott and I were just talking yesterday about, aesthetically, how nervous we are about this change," Crookes commented, "because the game has gotten a lot of really great feedback on how cosy it is, how beautiful the world is, and you're going to enter a game that is much more unforgiving and harsh at first glance."

That said, he thinks the shift "pairs really well with going into open alpha, because it is a much stronger breadcrumb [trail] for the player, to pull them into the world and give them a bit more ownership of what they're doing." Once rinsed of Ode siphons, regions will appear more like how they are in previous versions of Soulframe, with activities such as fishing and new resources to snaffle.

McGregor added that hitherto, a lot of Soulframe players have gotten lost and put the game down after completing the opening "Fables", or story quests. "It's a really big change to the structural flow of the game, you know," he told the assembled journorabble. "We're very open and discoverable, and we had a lot of player feedback that was basically 'what do I do next? What do I do next? I don't know what to do next'.

"So [it's] taking that and mashing it with the votive system, which is our mission system for the game, and making that more of a directed experience," he went on, "and then once they get through that directed experience, they can go back to that open world." Prelude 17 will also let you accept votives more straightforwardly from the world map, after finding the local representative or mission giver.

Digital Extremes have a new Soulframe "pact" or character loadout on the boil, the Ode Shrike. It's a dastardly poacher class who specialises in spike traps and throwable bolas. The Shrike's standout ability is a balloon dart that lets you hoist enemies into the sky, as in Metal Gear Solid V.

You can read more about Soulframe's on-going reinventions on the official site. While you won't need a key to get access as of Nov 6th, the game's paid Founders program will remain the same. Digital Extremes will likely still run closed preview builds alongside the "open prelude", testing out features with a smaller group of players. They're also looking into giving you the ability to reset your character, so you can check out any new material added to parts of the game you've finished.

I'm not sure I've ever been exhilarated by Soulframe, but I like the poise, flamboyance and gentle complexity of its combat. I also really enjoy its faded tapestry aesthetics, though I think it's yanking on the goo-goo glands too avidly with all these fluffy forest animals. Enough photogenic wolfpups, Digital Extremes - let's see you make, I don't know, a blobfish look adorable.

It's also very interesting as a new live service project from a company defined by the success of Warframe. I spoke to the Soulframe developers earlier in the year about the challenge of borrowing Warframe's thunder without getting lost in its shadow.

Funcom will also "continue expanding the game" through 2027.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Thus far, Funcom has focussed mainly on changes to its survival MMO Dune: Awakening, with the Norwegian studio reworking the entire game to function as both a solo experience and a PvE adventure. Now that overhaul is done, however, Funcom is now set on expanding players' adventures on Arrakis, having just announced a free expansion that adds a new and completely different map to explore.

Coming in December, the Blood and Ice DLC will let players depart the searing sands of Arrakis for the planet's frozen north, adding a new survival map called the Polar Sink that flips the game's central survival concept on its head. Rather than avoiding the heat, players will actively have to seek it out, while also developing new technologies to help them adapt to the extreme change in climate.

There's some variance within this environment too. The Polar Sink is composed of two different biomes, the tundra and the icecap. While the icecap is the more extreme of the two, both areas are closely guarded by "water shippers", wealthy traders who supply Arrakis' second most-valuable resource from the polar regions down to the deserts. Players' primary objective in the DLC will be breaking the water shippers' stranglehold on the ice, which they can then use to cool their base equipment back in the desert and speed up resource production.

Funcom says that the expansion adds "around 35 hours of new progression", which sounds pretty beefy for a free DLC. It also apparently "brings the focus back to ground-level survival" for veteran players, "traversal, temperature management and combat all playing important roles in your progression."

Blood and Ice will be released on December 1. Alongside the expansion, Funcom has also introduced a Cosmetics Store to Awakening, and is also working on several other heavily requested features. These include an offline single-player mode that's coming in November (the game can be played solo right now, but only with an Internet connection) and fully supported cross-play in January next year.

Funcom also says that Blood and Ice represents "another step in the ongoing development of Dune: Awakening" and that it will "continue expanding the game" through 2027. This falls in line with the studio's recent announcement that it was pivoting to exclusively support its existing games—which includes Conan Exiles alongside Dune: Awakening—and was laying off an unspecified number of employees as a result of that shift in strategy.

#3911. Palworld studio still hopes to release the game on Switch 2 one day, despite being in a legal battle with Nintendo

Palworld, the survival crafting game featuring adorable animals seemingly inspired by Pokémon, has been embroiled in a legal battle with Nintendo over what the company alleges is patent infringement. But although the lawsuit is ongoing, Palworld developer Pocketpair still says it's keen to bring the game to Switch 2.

Speaking to VGC, Pocketpair CEO Takuru Mizobe said he "of course" wants to bring the game to Nintendo's console. "First of all, I should say that we think the Switch 2 is a really amazing platform, not just for games globally, but especially here in Japan and for the Japanese games industry. It's been an incredible platform.

"If there's ever a future where we have the opportunity to discuss or consider bringing Palworld to the Switch platform in some way, then we'd love to have those conversations."

This stance isn't particularly surprising; Mizobe previously said it would be difficult to bring Palworld to the original Switch given how demanding the game is, but that could change if Switch 2 - the specs of which had yet to be revealed - has hardware capable enough to run the game. One year later, Pocketpair communications director John Buckley told IGN that a Switch 2 port was worth considering, assuming the console could handle the game.

Still, technical capabilities aside, we're not likely to see Palworld on Switch 2 until the lawsuit between Pocketpair and Nintendo is resolved. We're scheduled to hear an update on it soon, as the Tokyo District Court is set to issue a preliminary view on 9th November.

Palworld has sold over 30 million copies since its release in 2024, with July's 1.0 update attracting almost 1 million concurrent players on Steam.

If you were hoping to do some invading and such in Dark Souls 2 or 3 over the weekend, you would've seen that those features are currently disabled. Servers have been shut down for both games, but fear not; it's a temporary measure to fix some issues on FromSoftware's end, though a return date hasn't been set.

Online features for both installments of the Dark Souls series suddenly went down on Friday, October 30, after a brief warning per FromSoftware. At the time, the only explanation was that an issue had been discovered, and no timeline was given for when they'd be back up.

Fast forward now to Monday, November 2, and there's been a small update. Servers on Dark Souls 2 and 3 "have been temporarily suspended for all platforms due to identified security vulnerabilities," reads the post. "We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. Thank you for your patience and understanding."

Due to a server issue, the game servers for the following titles will be temporarily unavailable on all platforms. We will provide updates once we have information regarding the server restoration time. We apologize for the inconvenience. DARK SOULS II DARK SOULS IIIOctober 30, 2026

It's clarified that this includes every platform, and it means the games can't be played in online mode whatsoever. Offline is still completely fine.

This might be frustrating for some Dark Souls 2 players in particular, because that game went offline during the week for what appeared to be routine maintenance. It only came back on October 28 before going down again.

That's an annoying coincidence if that's been your entry of choice for trolling others or helping weaker players out. Without an explanation it's hard to say what's actually going on, but hopefully there hasn't been any kind of actual cyber-attack and the devs are simply fixing up the existing patchwork to be more robust.

These games have been out for over a decade, they need to be kept up to date. Thankfully, Form is doing that, you might just need to head back to Firelink Shrine for a minute before getting to play them again.

#3908. What are we all playing this weekend?

My scares should have been reserved for today, what with it being All Hallows' Eve and all, but my fright came on Thursday.

It was a dark October night and I was returning from work. A storm had blown through earlier in the week, so the evening was unusually crisp and clear. I walked between the terrace houses, feeling the eyes of work-from-homers on my back. I turned the key in the door to the communal hallway, climbed the creaky stairs, and tried to keep my footsteps light as I passed my rude neighbour's flat. My head was wholly absorbed by the prospect of the risotto I had waiting in the fridge/

I unlocked my front door and started up the internal staircase to the kitchen, not even bothering to turn on the lights. Out of the dark, something jumped down the stairs at me, hitting me in the stomach. I flicked the lights on in a panic and saw a small brown thing with a long tail bolting back up the staircase. A mouse. In my house.

Terrifying stuff, I'm sure you will agree. It almost put me off my risotto. Anyway, this is what the rest of the team will be up to this weekend..

OllieI've settled into a very comfy rhythm of playing the latest Trackmania campaign and also a bit of Factorio, both with my brother. When I've a bit of time to myself I'm also interested in trying out Queen's Domain. Heard good things!

JeremyI continue to chip away at our Castlevania walkthrough as it chips away at my soul. Such is the transactional bargain of dealing with Dracula during Halloween, no? However, as I answer the door for trick-or-treaters, I may partake in what is becoming an annual tradition - watching an old game playthrough on YouTube as I hand out sweets. I'm thinking I will watch the 1994 SNES game Nosferatu this year, which is not related to Castlevania but does feature a bold guy going to beat up Dracula and all of his minions with nothing but his feet and fists.

JamesMy previously mentioned attempts to play Mortal Shell 2 have been thwarted this week by, in chronological order, work, social obligations, brownie making, Deep Rock Galactic, and more brownie making. We go again.

EdwinI'm helping with a house move this weekend, so I doubt I'll have much time for your foolish computer entertainments, but I'd like to crack on with Queen's Domain and also, try out Danchi Days, a sorrowful comedy about trying to revive a summer festival in a 2000s-era Japanese neighbourhood.

CallumSuspiciously, Callum has been making squeaking noises in meetings. Is this a sign he planted the mouse? Perhaps he was the mouse. Surely, it's not a coincidence. There's no such thing as coincidence when it comes to mice.

MarkI want to finish Virtue and a Sledgehammer, having started it the other night. I really dug The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood, one of Spanish studio Deconstructeam's previous games. Thus far, VaaS is hitting just as hard in terms of emotional beats, but in a manner that's more haunting than charming. We'll see where I land on it by the end.

JulianAs well as searching my flat for mouse hidey holes, I will be (touch wood/cross fingers/make a sacrifice to Bob the Builder) finishing the DIY I started last weekend. Alcove bookcases and a painted living room are in my future, I just have to manifest it.

Besides that, I've been dipping my toes into Titanium Court. I like it but I don't so far love it. It's witty, the presentation is excellent, but I feel like it is also keeping me at arm's length and I want to be drawn into its world, not kept at a distance. It may just need more time. I will also be trying hard not to sweep the moon.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

#3907. Tales of Tuscany launches February 22, 2027

Tales of Tuscany, a “WarioWare-soaked open-world RPG” follow-up to the 2024-released Athenian Rhapsody, will launch for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, Switch, PC via Steam, iOS, and Android on February 22, 2027, publisher Top Hat Studios and developer Nico Papalia announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via Top Hat Studios:

Tuscany has been obliterated by the evil wizard Thunder Goober for his own personal entertainment! Play as Lambypoo and adventure through the broken land of Tuscany, either making friends and having them join your team or defeating enemies for their EXP in your efforts to save your cousins and reunite Tuscany…

Each journey through Tuscany is completely unique to the player at the wheel, and you’ll be awarded something called a Rhapsody each time you complete the game—a postcard which details your entire playthrough which you can trade cross-platform between friends! You’re tasked with reuniting Tuscany, but nobody is telling you how… do whatever you want!

Tales of Tuscany is a fast-paced, hilarious RPG where you control your own story. Build a team of misfits to take on bosses with and make choices that shape the world around you! Features include…

Bla Bla Bla I’m a Sheep. Alright I Get That Part. What is Like, the Actual Story?

The world of Tuscany was an ancient, undisturbed land until the evil wizard Thunder Goober shattered through the atmosphere from the realm of Elysium—he then struck Tuscany with a giant bolt of lightning, completely obliterating your home town and sending all of your cousins flying all over the map! The hole in the atmosphere also began leaking EXP particles, which when collected by Tuscanos makes them stronger, but also crazy!

Now, Lambypoo has the chance to travel around Tuscany and save every cousin, which will help to rebuild new facilities at The Village—but Thunder Goober may have an underlying reason for causing all of this mayhem… No spoilers, you have to play the game! Hehe got you

Can You Explain the “Rhapsody” Part Again? (I Was on the Phone With My Mom, Sorry)

Okay listen up buster—this game is a choose-your-own-adventure, which means you can choose your own adventure. You can choose to collect an obscene amount of EXP, just a little bit, or none at all—you can choose to help or harm many characters around the world for reasons of your own and circumvent issues in more ways than one… Through all of these choices, a visual recreation of your Tale (in Tuscany) is created for you to bring into the real world and use to share your experience with friends. Tales of Tuscany is not meant to just be a singe-player-game, but also serve as a communication tool to share your experiences and compare/contrast amongst your friends, and even trade valuable keepsakes if you really trust each other.

Yes it’s so good. You can join a multi level marketing scheme, roll around a spicy dung-beetle-ball, get a corporate job, blow up cars, shoot your friends out of cannons so they explode, and there’s even a public pool. I know I mentioned that before but seriously who doesn’t like the public pool it’s the best place on earth…

#3906. Mass Effect composer wants to rescore leaked internal ME Universe trailer to "properly represent my musical vision"

Mass Effect trilogy composer Sam Hulick has expressed his intent to rescore the tantalising trailer for BioWare's cancelled Mass Effect Universe for N7 day.

Hulick shared this plan on X, writing: "Alright. My plan is to release the re-scored Mass Effect Universe trailer for N7 Day. A little tight, since I'm a bit busy pitching for a new game, but I'll see what I can do! I don't wanna rush it, and I want it to properly represent my musical vision for MEU."

The Mass Effect Universe trailer, released last week, was intended for EA and BioWare management to indicate what the now cancelled fifth Mass Effect game would be like. As such, the music and assets were not meant to be seen by the public, hence the rescore.

And it turns out that Hulick isn't the only musically-minded person to plan on releasing some Mass Effect Universe music. Prolific composer Austin Wintory - known for his work on Sword of the Sea, Journey, and Hades 2 - posted 20 minutes of music he shared with BioWare staff back in 2025 in the hopes of working on Mass Effect Universe.

Wintory and Hulick join many who decried the closure of BioWare last week, which impacted 50 employees there, and were a part of wider restructuring that affected hundreds of other people elsewhere in EA. This came only a few months after EA's acquisition by Saudi Arabia's Savvy Games Group and Jared Kushner's private equity firm.

#3905. Horror-steeped card game Forbidden Solitaire shows how a strong theme can elevate even decade-old mechanics

Like a tag team of oiled snakes that have entered a wrestling contest, theme is a difficult quality to pin down. A game can be well designed, but if it lacks a coherence between those mechanics and its appearance, narrative, and its framing, there is a dissonance that can be hard to ignore. I realise I've just stepped into an old argument by using the word 'dissonance', but Hocking was right, games that don't cohere can be jarring. A developer may desire that sensation of discomfort, but often it is accidental and unwanted.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

(Much like opening an article with a simile about wrestling snakes when there is nothing connecting that image to a game about solitaire. It might be a good line, but it doesn't smoothly connect with the rest of the article to elevate its argument.)

Anyway, what does this all have to do with Forbidden Solitaire, a game in which you're delving deeper into a dungeon filled with horrors, progressing by clearing screens of cards? Well, it's an excellent example of how well-handled theming can raise a game into something more than its parts.

I've been playing Grey Alien Games' work since they released Regency Solitaire in 2015, and their games often revolve around the same core, Solitaire-inspired mechanics. Each level is a screen filled with stacks of playing cards, and you must clear the screen by picking cards that are one higher or lower than the one currently in your hand. In addition to standard playing cards, you may find padlock cards which can only be cleared with a matching key card, special cards that reshuffle all the stacks, or ones that change cards into suits or numbers that may help you. Except, in each of their games – Regency Solitaire, Shadowhand, Ancient Enemy, and now Forbidden Solitaire - the scenario for those mechanics changes, and in doing do, they show the power of recontextualising.

In Forbidden Solitaire, you're playing a game within a game. Although it's set in 2019, your character is playing a 1995 CD-ROM they found in a second-hand shop. It's one you vaguely remember from your childhood, if mainly for the controversy it caused at launch. The game sees you breaking into an old dungeon and exploring its depths. Each locked door that blocks you, labyrinth that puzzles you, or enemy that challenges you is tackled with the mechanics of Grey Alien Games' previous releases: screens of stacked cards to be cleared. Even familiar special cards, such as the one which shuffles all the cards before you, make a return. As you progress through Forbidden Solitaire's dungeon, you're interrupted by messages from your sister in the present, who is researching the game and the controversy surrounding it, sending you links to police reports, old news clips of the secretive developer, and hidden documents on a centuries-old group of cultists.

Yet, despite the mechanical familiarity, it's this fresh theme that elevates Forbidden Solitaire into something special. For new players, the 1995 game framing device immediately gives an allowance for the simple card mechanics, and allows them to sink into the kitsch horror story of cult members developing haunted video games. But, for returning players like me, I can see all the neat ways the old tools have been adapted to fit this new world. When you find a person marked for sacrifice tied to a bed, for instance, the level to free them is filled with locks that only disappear when you match enough cards of the same suit. It's a pairing of unlocking mechanics that have been in Grey Alien Games' work for at least the past decade to a moment in the story where you are untying a character. The action dovetails with the narrative perfectly.

Anyway, when I realised the role that theme had to play in Forbidden Solitaire, I was feeling extremely smart and smug. Then I reread Adam (RPS in peace) and Pip's (RPS in peace) Regency Solitaire verdict from 2015.

Adam: I think the whole game is a superb example of how a decent design can be elevated by a strong theme. It’s not even particularly overindulgent - flourishes throughout but no extended dialogues or huge slabs of exposition. It’s a few attractive backgrounds (though with an inaccurate non-pebbled Brighton beach, I’m told by RPS chatroom stalwart and Brighton denizen Alec Meer), a handful of characters and miniature conversations to set the tone. But it’s all done so well. It seems to be aware of its own posture in a way that allows it to be well-mannered, well-meaning and not at all over-bearing.

If it had been pixies or space marines, I don’t think I’d have been particularly interested at all - and that’s not to say the actual card game isn’t well-constructed because it is - but even though the story is slight, it’s a great reward at the end of a few hands.

Pip: I'd agree with that, particularly about the setting. It's a game that has a good understanding of its own size, scope and the tone which suits it.

Those absolute cads. Still, go play Forbidden Solitaire anyway. It's a far better time than trying to get an oiled snake into a three-piece suit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Rick and Ted have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager.

If you've played an extraction shooter like Arc Raiders or Marathon, you've probably experienced the agony of trusting another player only for them to shoot you in the head and nick all your stuff. Whenever that happens—and it's happened to me more than I'd like to admit—the same questions run through my head (after the traditional wailing and gnashing of teeth). Was that always going to happen? Did I do something wrong? Should I have said something different? Behaved differently? Or should I have simply foregone any attempt at diplomacy and shot first?

I've often wondered if there's a way to get better at this. Not just to convince other players that I'm not a threat, but to make them not want to shoot me. Conveniently, I recently had the chance to speak to someone who knows a thing or two about resolving such situations, both in videogames and real life.

James 'Pigeon' Fielder is one of only two political scientists in the world who specialise in gaming. Or at least, if there are more than two, Fielder is yet to be made aware of them: "When I talk about my research with fellow political scientists they either look at me like I'm crazy or they go 'Oh, that sounds cool.'"

Political science is the study of governments, which in turns means it's the study of human behaviour at a large-scale, organised level. Areas of interest include policy development, power distribution, and most importantly for us, conflict resolution.

What relevance does this have to games? Fielder answers this himself: "It's almost like taking theories of political science and doing fruit fly experiments, like trying to understand human behaviour, specifically human political behaviour, inside of game worlds," he says. "In a space like EVE Online, we might see political phenomena develop in weeks, months, or years that in real life would take decades or centuries to express themselves."

How does one become a political scientist specialising in games? Well, it's not exactly a job with an established career path, but Fielder arrived at it through his career in the US military, where his lifelong love of TTRPGs resulted in an aptitude for designing wargames. "I was getting groomed to be promoted from specialist to sergeant, and to be promoted, I had to demonstrate that I could teach a class," he says. "So I decided to build a class on a task that integrated roleplaying game elements. Why it seemed like a good idea at the time, I can't recall. All I know is that everybody had a great time."

Fielder's commanding officers took notice: "Once you get that stink on you in the military, like 'Oh Fielder, can you build another exercise for us?' You build another exercise, and they would get bigger and bigger," he says. "To date, the biggest exercise I've ever designed was for 5,000 people that ran 168 hours."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Fielder eventually switched from the US Army to the US Air Force and was hired by the Air Force Academy to teach political science. "My degrees are in history and national security … but it was political science who hired me." During a lesson on social capital or "why do people trust each other" as Fielder puts it, one student asked a question—can people develop trust in online games the same way they do in person?

"Like a good scientist, I went 'Huh, I don't know. Let me look that up," Fielder says. "That's when I started learning why games are so effective at bringing people together."

To very briefly summarise why games are effective in this manner: while the scenarios games present are fictional, the feelings they produce in the people playing them are very real. Anyone who has rage-quit a game will understand this. But games are also capable of producing more complex emotions and imagined states of being.

With roleplaying games in particular, they encourage people to inhabit personalities and mental states other than their own. In the right circumstances, these feelings can help instil empathy or new perspectives in people. "A [prison] inmate, for example, might put on the character of a lawful good hero," Fielder posits. "Now, when I'm supposed to be stealing from people, or using violence or vandalism, I'm going to play a Paladin, and now I'm inculcating what it's like to be a lawful good Paladin. I get debriefed at the end of the game, and I go 'Oh, it actually felt good. It felt good to be playing that different person.'"

Fielder has applied these techniques in a military context, such as forecasting the outcome of elections in Afghanistan as he discussed in a 2023 TeDX talk. But since retiring from the military, he's also applied these techniques in a civilian context, running games and exercises for businesses, prisons, and other institutions.

What's especially interesting, though, is that the lessons learned from playing out scenarios in the real world can then feed back into games and game design. To take the latter first, alongside his political science work, Fielder is also an RPG designer and design consultant: "When I run games at conventions and I run one shots, if it's an invention that I've designed, I work to try to maximise the amount of agency players have," he says.

"Players want to feel like they're powerful and can do something cool, even if it's an unforgiving setting like Call of Cthulhu …. Where the lethality is high, players like to think that the decisions they make matter, and when they do, when the dice work against them and they can see the dice fall, they're more likely to accept it as fair."

Likewise, players can deploy techniques for deescalation and establishing trust used in the real world in games too, which is where we circle back to extraction shooters. Fielder starts by pointing out that the rules of the game must support cooperation to begin with. "If it's a game like the original iteration of PUBG, then that's impossible because you know that 'The only way to win is I have to kill everybody.'"

This might seem obvious. But it's also applicable on a sliding scale—the more explicit and involved the rules are for cooperation, the more likely players will use them. This is why you're more likely to see cooperation in Arc Raiders than Marathon. While Marathon has the capacity for cooperative play, this idea hasn't filtered through to the playerbase in the way it did with Arc Raiders, perhaps because of its faster TTK, or its friendly callout being less clear than Arc Raiders' 'Don't Shoot!'

But assuming that the rules apply and there's at least a base level of comprehension. "The best way—it's not foolproof—is to approach without visible weapons. If there's a way to have an emoticon where you can have your hands outstretched … and this comes from my military background, [it] demonstrates 'Look, my hands are empty, and it's very difficult for me to grab a weapon, even in a videogame.'"

In addition, Fielder says trust is established a lot faster if you have something to offer and offer it freely. "I don't expect anything in return except let's not fight," he says. "The more valuable that item is, the more receptive your audience will be." He concedes that there is a risk here. "If you offer something very valuable they [might] go, 'Oh, maybe he has more stuff.'"

Fielder has spent much of his life studying and using games as a method to resolve conflict. But there is one area of conflict where a solution still eludes him, and that's within the gaming community itself. "It actually hurts me when I see social differences in the gaming space, gatekeepers over racial differences, gender differences, or players [who] are angered with each other," he says.

"In reality, one of the best places to overcome differences with people is a game. You learn, you sit down to play, you work together to overcome an objective," Fielder continues. "Gaming should be the most inclusive space in the world. And why it's not always that case, I don't know."

#3903. Valve addresses Steam's AI game cloning problem - by suggesting developers make their games less copyable

"Rather than relying on a single mechanic that someone can easily copy..."

Valve has responded to the worrying trend of games being cloned using generative-AI and sold on Steam, but instead of admonishing those games or promising to do something about them, it appears to have put the onus on developers to make their games less copyable.

Valve's business team members Tom Giardino and Marc Wilkinson were reportedly asked at a Steam Indie Connect developer conference in Korea, reported by InvenGlobal, whether Steam had any protective measures in place to stop games being cloned by AI. The questioner, a developer, cited an example whereby developers were held to ransom by people threatening to clone a game.

It was in response that example that Giardino - after saying this was the first he'd heard of ransoming, and that probably it was an issue for law enforcement, though Valve would "help in whatever way we can" - outlined not what Valve was doing to clamp down on this, but what developers could do to guard against it. Indeed, Giardino began by underlining Valve's hands-off stance towards AI use, reportedly stating: "We don't want to be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn't use."

Instead, developers can guard against copycats by building active communities and establishing trust and by making a legitimate version of a game the best version available, Giardino reportedly said. Then there's the game itself: a more complex game will be harder to copy. "Rather than relying on a single mechanic that someone can easily copy, you need to keep growing your game by adding features, personality, and creativity that stem from your own perspective," Giardino reportedly said.

It's worth remembering Valve's comments here come second-hand, and via machine translation which InvenGlobal has separately verified with a native Korean speaker; we're asking Valve for clarification. But they also come after the widely publicised case of Needle in a Haystack Simulator, a simple indie game which isn't even out yet, but has been copied so many times it's hard to know which game is the original. The game's developer has resorted to joking that they're implementing a new game mode where you have to find the original game amidst a pile of copycats.

Without Valve's intervention, it's hard to see what a developer can do to guard against this. How can you build a community and trust, and ensure your game is the best version available, if you're not given a chance at finding an audience to begin with?

Plus, the sheer number of copycats makes this a whack-a-mole situation for containment, which is something that - without Valve's help - probably requires expensive legal resources anyway, which in turn is probably out of reach for many indie developers. Also, legal reprimands usually don't occur until long after the damage has been done.

This wouldn't be the first time Valve has distanced itself from moderating what's sold on its PC platform. Indeed in 2018, amidst growing concern about the kinds of games available on Steam, Valve seemed to back away entirely from taking responsibility.

"We've decided that the right approach is to allow everything onto the Steam Store," Valve's Erik Johnson said at the time, "except for things that we decide are illegal, or straight up trolling." It's a stance that former Eurogamer editor Oli called "arrogant and cowardly".

More recently, the pendulum swung the other way when Valve threw an undiscerning net over an entire sector of 'adult' games, catching in it a slew of well-meaning, artistically mature games, as well as those of a more crass nature. And with Steam growing every year, and more games being released on the platform than ever before, the everpresent issue of moderation is certainly not going to disappear.

#3902. The Sunday Papers

Sundays are for looking upon my DIY works and despairing. Strewn sawdust, spilled paint, and hunks of broken MDF litter my living room kingdom. When will it be over? When will I be free? When will I be able to reassemble my sofa, sit down with a cup of tea in hand, and admire my books, unpacked and arranged on perfectly fitted alcove bookshelves?

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

"Today?" I whisper hopefully in response to a paragraph of rhetorical questions. "Probably not," snaps back Reality. Especially if I don't get out of bed soon. Still, here in bed I can read the best writing about and not about games from the past week.

Inside our Gchat walls, there is a growing exhaustion with genAI stories. Every day another gaming boss talks about the inexorable march of the tech before putting out a trailer filled with blurry text and six-fingered characters. I don't doubt the tech is getting better, but it's not inevitable. As such, Rob Fahey's latest GI column is something of a balm:

There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.

At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.

A further tonic comes from Merritt K, who writes for Aftermath about the technological improvements rolling through Karaoke.

Doesn't it feel like everything — especially everything Big Tech touches — is getting worse? Generative AI, not merely content with robbing humans of our craft and jobs, has escaped containment into physical reality in the form of shitty event flyers and small business signage. Hugely profitable industries like video games and film are being torn apart by the financialization of the economy as shareholders seek ever-increasing short-term profits. Algorithmic pricing of rent and groceries threatens to further punish the working class for the crime of not being born rich.

But in the heart of despair, we must reach for that which is good and pure and — dare I say it — better than it used to be. Karaoke is one of those things. And it is better not because of the disruption of tech giants, but, as is often the case, thanks to the work of enterprising maniacs toiling in obscurity, purely out of the love of the game.

I've been playing Forbidden Solitaire this week, where FMV sequences starring Xalavier Nelson Jr as an obsessive fantasy-author-turned-video-game-developer are played for laughs. So it was with a minor sense of whiplash I read Ashley Bardhan's piece for This Week In Video Games. Bardhan speaks to horror developers inserting themselves into FMV games to confront and explore violence against women.

Cara Cadaver uses her own photos and videos to represent multiple victims of sexual violence and murder in her unflinching 2025 game Vile: Exhumed. She tells me over email, “Being a woman is inherently a horrifying and violent experience, any way you slice it. One of my inspirations for making games in general is pulling from real-life experience and telling stories that most every woman has lived in some way; that’s real horror.”

“Horror in general has been a major outlet for me while dealing with trauma, and so much of horror as a genre goes back to women,” Cadaver says. “Women’s stories belong in horror — and that has been the case as long as horror has existed.”

Over at RPS-but-it's-The-Fade, Brendan's run through what made Bioware games great (and also terrible).

Bioware established romance as a must for any blockbuster RPG worth its frost salts (and not just RPGs).

Kissing your friends on the mouth is everywhere in mainstream and indie games today. It's a verb now. Characters are "romanceable". I played Nivalis Nights last month and could not get away from the swarms of horny NPC citizens trying to jump my noodle serving bones. Baldur's Gate 3 launched with a bug that made your companions fuckable in just a few nights, and people didn't even notice. They thought: that's normal and right, I should shag everyone, gender and orientation be damned. See that mountain? You can fuck it. And that's (at least partially) thanks to Bioware.

GTA is an unignorable thing. It is one of those breakout cultural objects that has its own gravity, drawing in attention and comment from politicians, mainstream press, parents, schools, comedians, columnists, footballers, taxi drivers, and hairdressers. In all the weight of it, I hadn't yet really seen it as a game. Simon Parkin's Edge cover feature may not reveal many new details about the game but it has made me appreciate it as a game (and maybe even get a little bit excited for its eventual PC release.

Nelson, grave-faced but friendly, wearing all black, with grey-flecked stubble, settles into a leather-and-chrome Eames chair while we perch on a burnt-orange sofa facing a pair of expansive wall-mounted TVs. In the past, Rockstar has carefully stage-managed encounters such as this. For previews of previous GTAs, one team member played the game while a publicist read from a pre-prepared script, further evidence of the paranoia that can take hold when an artist is working on something the entire world is desperate to see.

Today, however, Nelson has no script and, apparently, no plan. For the next 90 minutes he simply plays the current build, following his nose, confident that the game's systems will hold together wherever he pushes them, that this world's glories will glint and shimmer no matter which angle he approaches from. It is an extraordinary demonstration not of paranoia but of trust – in the game, in the team that built it, perhaps even in us.

Nelson picks up the controller and lets Grand Theft Auto VI speak for itself.

I am guilty of forgetting and looking away, but the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has not ended, it is deepening. Writing for the LRB, Selma Dabbagh bluntly captures the ugly events of the past two years :

In January 2025 Donald Trump described Gaza as a ‘demolition site’. ‘You’re talking about probably a million and a half people,’ he said, ‘and we just clean out that whole thing.’ The number is closer to two million people – not a ‘whole thing’ but two million individual human beings – who have been driven into an area that’s less than a third of the densely inhabited land they lived on. Their cities and arable lands – palms, olives, coriander, citrus and pomegranate trees – have been obliterated.

I'd like there to be a big reason for this week's music recommendation, but really it's just a little victory lap. I managed to nab some tickets to see This Is The Kit, so give Bashed Out a listen, yeah?

Eiji Aonuma says "we were reminded once again just how important those moments are" to Ocarina of Time's structure

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's long-awaited Switch 2 remake might be bringing Nintendo's 1998 classic back to life with almost 28 years' worth of improvements, but the devs decided to reject one modern quality-of-life feature to avoid Link's classic adventure from losing some of its old magic.

Speaking in a new Nintendo Ask the Developer interview, Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma explains that during the development of the new remake, he suggested implementing a Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild-style quality-of-life feature that could have made traversing the world much quicker – fast-travel points.

"In The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, there are many warp points that enable players to move quickly around the game's vast world," he begins. "In the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, you could get around a bit faster by spamming forward roll, so I think a lot of players spent their time doggedly rolling across Hyrule Field whenever they needed to be somewhere in a hurry. (Laughs)."

This is something that Aonuma initially felt "we needed to address" in the remake. "So I asked the team to add warp points that didn't exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts," he explains.

However, when the devs implemented this feature, the vibes were completely off, the producer continues. "When we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, 'Wait, what's this?'" he reasons.

"Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time," Aonuma says. "So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again. (Laughs)."

Even without the newly added fast-travel points, the Zelda devs have added another way to get around Hyrule quickly. Instead of doing his best Sonic impression and rolling around at the speed of sound, Link can now simply run. Oh, and he can jump now, too.

#3899. Capcom's golden streak continues as Onimusha and Pragmata sell well, but Monster Hunter Wilds conspicuously absent from financial report

Capcom has revealed updated sales figures for its new and successful games, including Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Pragmata, and Resident Evil Requiem. But for some reason, Monster Hunter Wilds is absent from the report.

Capcom's half-year report, for the period running 1st April to 30th September, saw growth in both revenue and profit across nearly all segments of the business. In games, much of that was driven by digital sales, which continue to account for the vast majority of the publisher's income.

The first half of FY2026 was especially strong for Capcom owing to the release of multiple critically acclaimed and financially successful titles. Onimusha: Way of the Sword has now sold over 1.7m copies, up from the 1m it sold at launch. Pragmata, another critical and financial hit, has grown its tally to 2.7m copies, more than double what it sold in its first two days of release. Resident Evil Requiem, meanwhile, has now surpassed 8.5m copies sold.

As part of the same report, Capcom also recorded its highest-ever number of unit sales for the first half of any fiscal year. This is attributed to Capcom's strong back-catalogue of titles, and regular sales and discounts.

But Capcom did not reference Monster Hunter Wilds sales at all in the report. The publisher did not share updated sales for the game, despite sharing a milestone for predecessor Monster Hunter: World, which is now well past 30m copies sold.

Although Wilds was incredibly successful at launch, the game's player base tapered off dramatically shortly afterwards. Capcom offered a sales update in last year's version of the same report, where it was revealed that MH Wilds had sold close to 11m copies overall, but the publisher hasn't offered an update since.

What does this mean - have sales slowed so significantly as to not be worth mentioning? Perhaps. But given that Wilds is coming to Switch 2 this December, and with the Ascendance expansion due for release next year, there's fuel in the tank yet.

#3898. It looks like footage of a Persona 1 remake has leaked, and if it's legit I really hope you don't hate the colour purple

I'm sure the artist formerly known as Prince would have loved it, at least

In this genAI world, every single leak that makes its way out into the world should be seen as more of a "leak" until proven otherwise. With that said, it does kind of seem like a remake of the first Persona game is on the way, with some footage supposedly leaking and showing it in action.

The leaked footage was shared yesterday to the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit, originally uploaded to the file-sharing site Gofile on Halloween, i.e. yesterday, i.e. October 31st. You will not at all be surprised to hear that, stylistically, it's incredibly in line with the vibe of contemporary Persona, a la the visual design established with Persona 5 that's been carried through to the Persona 3 and 4 remakes.

There's not a whole lot of footage to actually look at, just shy of two minutes all told. One bit shows the game's protagonist walking through a school at night before starting a battle. Again, the battle system looks like what you'd expect from Persona, being turn based and whatnot. The colour theme for this one is overwhelmingly purple, too, which at least lines up with the series' 25th anniversary artwork. What's perhaps slightly odd is that Persona 2's protagonist can be seen in battle; not sure if this is implying a combination of the two games, if two remakes are being made in tandem and it's a temporary use of assets, or if it's just an odd placeholder.

Persona 1 and 2 remakes wouldn't exactly be much of a surprise. Ashley interviewed series producer Kazuhisa Wada not too long ago, and he literally said "Persona 1 and 2 are something we’ll probably eventually do too." A knowing tease from Wada, perhaps? Who knows! Either way, the gameplay on display here looks believable, and Sega's leakier than a broken faucet (various Persona bits have leaked in the past too), so, something to keep an eye on at the very least, even if best taken with a pinch of salt.

How far is too far in a universe that constantly pushes gore to its limits?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"The first thing that got us debating was the necrophiliac scene in the first Outlast. We had a lot of conversations about do we do it? Are we going too far with this? And how does it make sense in this environment? That was a heated conversation."

There are many scenes from Outlast that are burned into my memory, The Groom's sequence in Outlast's Whistleblower DLC, the finger amputation from the first game, or perhaps it was landing on a bunch of baby bones in Outlast 2. There's quite a lot to pick from over two games, a DLC, and the live service The Outlast Trials. But if Philippe Morin, co-founder of Red Barrels, had to pick the scene that made the team really stop and think about whether this was ok he'd go back to the first game.

For those who don't remember, or perhaps have never played the game, or maybe just wiped the encounter from your memory, as the protagonist Miles Upshur is navigating the abandoned Mount Massive Asylum he stumbles across an inmate engaging in necrophilia. It's a pretty startling moment, and was actually the last thing I thought I'd come across, even in an Outlast game. But that was the whole point of that scene.

"We felt like we needed something that's going to make people think that anything can happen in this game," Morin explains. "Then J.T. Petty, [lead writer for Outlast] came up with this whole dialogue of switching things around, having the [necrophiliac] say to you, 'You like to watch? You're fucked up!' So that was a really nice spin because it turned things around. Because obviously, yes, the player is making the choice to watch. So yeah, I mean that's probably the very first sequence that got a bit [heated]."

The only other time Morin can recall where the team spent so long debating whether or not to include a scene actually happened more recently, in The Outlast Trials. Specifically, the decision to include child mannequins instead of animated children in trials like Grind the Bad Apples or Punish the Miscreants.

Morin explains how the team questioned "what to do with the kids? Do we make them mannequins, or do we have actual characters? At the end of the day it's a bunch of polygons moving. But you know, in the player's mind, it's not the same thing. That was probably where we found our limit. Like, no, let's stick with mannequin kids, and not go too far with that."

This was undoubtedly the right decision. There's plenty of extreme moments in The Outlast Trials with objectives like Pervert the Futterman or Despoil the Auction, the gore and horror already present is more than enough to make players feel uneasy as is—trust me.

But as it is with most games, the best decisions tend to be made by the people who know the series best; its devs. "The team is always the first to react to some of these ideas," Morin says. "So sometimes if people feel like it's alright, let's keep pushing in that direction until like maybe the reaction becomes a little too strong.

"I remember discussing at some point when we went from 20 people to 30-40 people, because most people on the team were not with us for Outlast or Outlast 2, so we had to have a little chat about what kind of conversations are necessary to create this kind of content?

"And sometimes, yes, it might start with a very juvenile, gratuitous idea, but then you have to let it evolve, and be willing to talk around it to come up with an approach that feels scary and satisfying. You gotta be able to have those conversations. We often joke about that at Red Barrels. There are many conversations that would take you to an HR office in other studios, but here it's just part of our daily routine."

#3896. Here are our PS Plus monthly games for November 2026

Dead Island 2! Tomb Raider! Monster Train 2!

Sony has announced the monthly games coming to PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra next month, bringing a mix of triple-A bangers and remastered classics to the service on the 3rd November. All are, of course, coming at the start of what is almost certainly going to be the biggest month of the year releases-wise.

Perhaps the biggest game on offer is Dead Island 2, Dambuster Studios and Deep Silver's first person zombie action game. There's plenty of grisly goodness here, and ample loot to snatch up and use against the undead hordes. It's a decent enough game, which should offer plenty of entertainment to those looking for something chunky to dig their teeth into while the Halloween spirit still lingers.

The remastered Tomb Raider Darkness Trilogy is not one to be skipped, especially if you're looking for a sizable time sink from your PlayStation Plus monthly games. While not known as being exactly the best Lara Croft games out there, Aspyr did some fine work polishing them up for modern platforms.

Finally we've got Monster Train 2. A deckbuilder roguelike that has you operating and managing trains where the forces of heaven and hell reside, all to defeat titans that threaten the orderly state of things. As the sole indie release on this monthly selection of PlayStation Plus games, it may be worth a try for those who can't get enough from the Roguelike genre even now. It even features a smug looking mushroom fella, how can you go wrong with that.

The reveal of these games coming to PlayStation Plus means the clock is ticking to grab October's offerings, many of which would fit well on the console of those getting into the spooky season.

Compatible games need full manual button mapping

Mounting holes didn't fully align with my seat

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

Anyone who’s followed Formula 1 in the last few years knows that a lot of the most interesting action happens in the midfield. There may not be as much attention or fanfare given to it, but look away from the leader, and there’s fierce battling going on all over the place. Sim racing has a similar situation brewing. Direct drive racing wheels for PC were previously reserved for the championship leaders, but in the last couple of years we’ve seen that technology filter quickly down the field.

PXN is one of the more recent names to take a run at that space. Best known for more budget wheels at the cheaper end of the grid, it launched a direct drive range of its own last year, with the VD4, VD6, and VD10 bases covering 4Nm, 6Nm, and 10Nm of torque respectively. The PXN VD6 Bundle in the middle comes in at a reasonable $379/£409 and includes a 6Nm wheelbase, a 280mm round wheel, a two-pedal set, and a desk clamp.

That lineup and price tag put the VD6 squarely up against the MOZA R5 and Logitech G RS50, both of which I've spent plenty of time with in the past. I've now been racing with the VD6 Bundle for a couple of weeks to see if PXN's hardware should have the leaders looking in their mirrors

Don’t tell my editor, but the design section of sim racing reviews almost writes itself at this stage. I could probably copy and paste a lot of my MOZA R3 words here and call it a day. The PXN VD6 follows the pack when it comes to design. It’s a pretty plain black cube with some go-faster fins down each side, inputs around the back, and a quick-release on the front. It’s a method that works for everyone else, and it’s equally as successful here.

I was also braced for the usual compromises of sim racing gear at this price, though in fairness I don't have any real complaints about the VD6 base itself. It’s weighty and solid, with an aluminium shell that both feels premium and assists with thermal management. The rest of the bundle is a step down. The round wheel that’s included in the box is fine, but it's not in the same class as the wheelbase, and the same goes for the pedals. They both do the job but certainly feel much more like an entry-level pair.

That’s where the PXN GT ONE wheel comes in. It’s a standalone 300mm GT-style wheel that’s $219/£219 on its own, or $469/£469 bundled with the VD6 base (if you want pedals, they’re another $89/£89 on top). I’ve been testing it alongside the bundled wheel and found myself not wanting to switch back. This is much more like it. The quality difference is apparent as soon as you open the box. It feels like a proper piece of kit and fully in line with the self-assured quality the wheelbase gives off. The rubber on the grips is comfortable and has a more grown-up vibe than the textured faux leather of the default wheel. There's a good weight and solidity to the rim, and I much prefer the feel of the GT ONE's buttons, all of which are fully backlit.

The VD6 sits in what I consider to be the direct drive sweet spot, delivering 6Nm of constant torque with peaks of 7Nm and a 24-bit encoder for precision. That's plenty for most amateur sim racers, particularly anyone new or stepping up from a gear or belt-driven wheel like the staple Logitech G923. The included W AS wheel has a modest yet reasonable 12 buttons laid out around the rim, along with a simple D-pad, two rotary encoders, and RPM lights. The shifter and clutch paddles on the back are aluminium and use Hall Effect sensors, which was a pleasant surprise.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

The GT ONE is in a different league entirely. There are still 12 buttons, though here they’re larger, backlit, and laid out in a more authentic way than on the W AS, which leans more like an arcade controller than a simulation tool. PXN includes a sticker sheet in the box, too, so you can customize each button with a clear label. These sit alongside three rotary encoders on the main face, two thumb encoders, and two directional sticks, with magnetic shift paddles, Hall effect clutch paddles, and a row of RPM LEDs along the top. The brass-colored thumb encoders are great, though it's a shame they only twist and don't push too for a bonus input.

I’m less fond of the three rotary encoders on the front. They're too light for my liking, and I found them easy to overshoot the setting you wanted, particularly if only looking to turn them a single step.

The PD HM pedals are a pretty simple two-pedal set, though you can add a separate clutch pedal at a later date if you so wish. Both pedals use Hall effect sensors, meaning no load cell braking, and the resistance feels relatively light on both. They connect to the wheelbase via an onboard USB hub on the back, which also has a couple of spare ports for additional accessories like a shifter or button box. Like so much sim racing gear, the PXN VD6 Bundle is PC only with no console support whatsoever.

Rather than use the included desk mount, I bolted the VD6 to my Playseat Trophy Logitech G Edition, which has taken a bunch of other direct drive wheelbases without complaint. Here, however, I couldn't find a set of holes in the mounting plate that simultaneously lined up with the four bolt holes on the bottom of the PXN. I could only get a couple in any position I tried, and while this did hold firm enough, it isn't ideal. The pedals were the same, and arguably worse. There was always a little bit of play, particularly in heavy braking zones. Oh, and one tip: make sure to plug in all of your pedal cables before you mount them to a rig. Doing it afterwards without unbolting everything is incredibly fiddly, and no, I won't be taking questions on how I know that.

Getting racing also took far longer than it should have and is an area where it becomes apparent you’ve strayed away from a market-leading brand. Updating firmware across all parts of the bundle turned into a solid hour of faff, with the pedals going from recognized to not recognized and the GT ONE refusing to show up at all until the wheelbase was updated. Update one thing, and the app would tell me another component had rolled back. I had to roll back and start over multiple times before it finally seemed to stick. Things are fine now, mercifully, and the most recent wheelbase update went through smoothly, so fingers crossed PXN has got things in order.

I spent most of my time in the EA SPORTS F1 25: 2026 Season Pack, Forza Horizon 6, and EA WRC, all of which are listed as compatible in PXN’s documentation. Sadly, as is so often the case, every one needed manual configuration and button mapping, even when I'd used the PXN app to supposedly set things up first. It's irritating. The brighter news is that with buttons mapped, everything worked reliably and force feedback came through in every game. I did need to spend a while tinkering in Forza Horizon 6 to dial in the driving experience, and it was a case of trial and error. This isn’t an isolated PXN issue; I’ve found it tricky to get the balance right on other wheels in the past, but don’t expect to immediately hit the streets of Tokyo.

On track, 6Nm never felt short at my level and offered plenty of resistance to lean on around long corners. Truth be told, I only ever crank a stronger wheel like the Logitech G Pro up to maximum oomph for a laugh when someone new sits down, and I fancy freaking them out. You won’t need more than 6Nm for casual day-to-day racing. The force feedback is respectable and gets better the rougher the surface is. Riding a kerb or dipping a wheel into the gravel is always obvious, and there's enough detail to know what the car is doing. On the smooth parts, where you're meant to be in F1 25: 2026 Season Pack, there's less going on, though there's some sensation on standard tarmac, which is more than I got from the Turtle Beach KD3. It isn't best in class. The Logitech RS50 and G Pro are still the best I've used thanks to TRUEFORCE, but there's enough difference between surfaces to leave me feeling dialed in and immersed.

For what it delivers, it has to be said that the VD6 Bundle is good value. At $379/£409 for the full wheel, wheelbase, and pedal set, it's going wheel to wheel with the MOZA R5 and comfortably undercuts the likes of the Nacon Revosim RS Pure. I’d say the wheelbase is better than that price suggests, though the wheel and pedals don't quite reach that same level.

The GT ONE is a clear upgrade and one I highly recommend for track racers, though it skews the value proposition pretty dramatically. The VD6 and GT ONE bundle is $469/£469 without pedals, and the PD HM pedals add another $89/£89, so a full setup comes to somewhere near $560/£560. In the UK, that puts it level with a Logitech RS50 bundle including the track wheel and pedals, which is £550 in Logitech's configurator. The US doesn’t see as good a deal; the same set comes to $750 there. The GT ONE is a nicer wheel than the one in that bundle, but the RS50 has a load cell brake, a smoother app experience and game compatibility, and the best force feedback I've tested with TRUEFORCE.

If you're a PC racer after a direct drive bundle on a budget, and you're prepared to spend time on firmware and button mapping, the VD6 Bundle is easy to recommend. The overall experience is ultimately good; you’ll just have to take the scenic route to get there.

I tested the PXN VD6 Bundle and PXN GT ONE wheel on PC, mounted to a Playseat Trophy Logitech G Edition. I used both the included wheel and the GT ONE, alongside the PD HM pedals, across EA SPORTS F1 25: 2026 Season Pack, Forza Horizon 6, and EA WRC. Everything was set up and configured through the PXN SimRacing app, updating the firmware as prompted and required.

A week ago, I asked PC Gamer readers to nominate the scariest PC games they could think of. I collected the top 16 submissions from that comment section (with some editorial discretion) and randomly seeded a bracket.

After a week of voting, we've finally got a winner. The scariest game on PC is...

Some of you called it from the start, and Alien: Isolation plowed through its competition without much resistance, beating SOMA, Darkwood, Silent Hill 2, and finally Amnesia: The Dark Descent.

Having a Xenomorph stalker is scary: reconfirmed. "Alien: Isolation completely destroys me, drenching me in sweat and causing me to take leave of my senses," Fraser wrote a couple years ago. It took him 10 years to get up the courage to finish it.

This article is brought to you by No More Room in Hell 2.

Our runner up is classic first-person horror game Amnesia: The Dark Descent, which entered the final after a close battle with one of its younger siblings, Amnesia: The Bunker.

Solid arguments were made for the scariness of The Bunker, which Ted once said is the scariest game he's ever played, but The Dark Descent was a landmark PC horror game that lodged itself in a lot of our memories 16 years ago as a very scary thing that once happened to us.

Speaking to PC Gamer back in 2010, Frictional Games co-founder Thomas Grip said that their strategy was "to hint at things and then let the players build up an image in their head."

If you haven't played any of these games, it's a good time to pick them up. Alien: Isolation is $10 on Steam right now, and Amnesia: The Dark Descent is just $4.
